#10843. Scientists create smart synthetic skin that can hide images and change shape

Synthetic materials are widely used across science, engineering, and industry, but most are designed to perform only a narrow range of tasks. A research team at Penn State set out to change that. Led by Hongtao Sun, assistant professor of industrial and manufacturing engineering (IME), the group developed a new fabrication technique that can produce multifunctional "smart synthetic skin." These adaptable materials can be programmed to perform a wide variety of tasks, including hiding or revealing information, enabling adaptive camouflage, and supporting soft robotic systems.

Using this new approach, the researchers created a programmable smart skin made from hydrogel, a soft, water-rich material. Unlike conventional synthetic materials with fixed behaviors, this smart skin can be tuned to respond in multiple ways. Its appearance, mechanical behavior, surface texture, and ability to change shape can all be adjusted when the material is exposed to external triggers such as heat, solvents, or physical stress.

The findings were published in Nature Communications, where the study was also selected for Editors' Highlights.

Inspired by Octopus Skin and Living Systems

Sun, the project's principal investigator, said the concept was inspired by cephalopods such as octopuses, which can rapidly alter the look and texture of their skin. These animals use such changes to blend into their surroundings or communicate with one another.

"Cephalopods use a complex system of muscles and nerves to exhibit dynamic control over the appearance and texture of their skin," Sun said. "Inspired by these soft organisms, we developed a 4D-printing system to capture that idea in a synthetic, soft material."

Sun also holds affiliations in biomedical engineering, material science and engineering, and the Materials Research Institute at Penn State. He described the process as 4D printing because the printed objects are not static. Instead, they can actively change in response to environmental conditions.

Printing Digital Instructions Into Material

To achieve this adaptability, the team used a method called halftone-encoded printing. This technique converts image or texture data into binary ones and zeros and embeds that information directly into the material. The approach is similar to how dot patterns are used in newspapers or photographs to create images.

By encoding these digital patterns within the hydrogel, the researchers can program how the smart skin reacts to different stimuli. The printed patterns determine how various regions of the material respond. Some areas may swell, shrink, or soften more than others when exposed to temperature changes, liquids, or mechanical forces. By carefully designing these patterns, the team can control the material's overall behavior.

"In simple terms, we're printing instructions into the material," Sun explained. "Those instructions tell the skin how to react when something changes around it."

One of the most eye-catching demonstrations involved the material's ability to conceal and reveal visual information. Haoqing Yang, a doctoral candidate in IME and the paper's first author, said this capability highlights the potential of the smart skin.

To demonstrate the effect, the team encoded an image of the Mona Lisa into the hydrogel film. When the material was washed with ethanol, it appeared transparent and showed no visible image. The hidden image became clear only after the film was placed in ice water or gradually heated.

Yang noted that the Mona Lisa was used only as an example. The printing technique allows virtually any image to be encoded into the hydrogel.

"This behavior could be used for camouflage, where a surface blends into its environment, or for information encryption, where messages are hidden and only revealed under specific conditions," Yang said.

The researchers also showed that concealed patterns could be detected by gently stretching the material and analyzing how it deforms using digital image correlation analysis. This means information can be revealed not only visually, but also through mechanical interaction, adding an extra level of security.

The smart skin also demonstrated remarkable flexibility. According to Sun, the material can easily shift from a flat sheet into complex, bio-inspired shapes with detailed surface textures. Unlike many other shape-changing materials, this transformation does not require multiple layers or different substances.

Instead, the changes in shape and texture are controlled entirely by the digitally printed halftone patterns within a single sheet. This allows the material to replicate effects similar to those seen in cephalopod skin.

Building on this capability, the team showed that multiple functions can be programmed to work together. By carefully designing the halftone patterns, they encoded the Mona Lisa image into flat films that later transformed into three-dimensional forms. As the sheets curved into dome-like shapes, the hidden image slowly appeared, showing that changes in shape and visual appearance can be coordinated within one material.

"Similar to how cephalopods coordinate body shape and skin patterning, the synthetic smart skin can simultaneously control what it looks like and how it deforms, all within a single, soft material," Sun said.

Expanding the Potential of 4D-Printed Hydrogels

Sun said the new work builds on earlier research by the team on 4D-printed smart hydrogels, which was also published in Nature Communications. That earlier study focused on combining mechanical properties with programmable transitions from flat to three-dimensional forms. In the current research, the team expanded the approach by using halftone-encoded 4D printing to integrate even more functions into a single hydrogel film.

Looking ahead, the researchers aim to create a scalable and versatile platform that allows precise digital encoding of multiple functions within one adaptive material.

"This interdisciplinary research at the intersection of advanced manufacturing, intelligent materials and mechanics opens new opportunities with broad implications for stimulus-responsive systems, biomimetic engineering, advanced encryption technologies, biomedical devices and more," Sun said.

The study also included Penn State co-authors Haotian Li and Juchen Zhang, both doctoral candidates in IME, and Tengxiao Liu, a lecturer in biomedical engineering. H. Jerry Qi, professor of mechanical engineering at Georgia Institute of Technology, also collaborated on the project.

#10842. Pokemon unveils Red and Green Fender guitars with special 8-bit sound feature

Pokemon has announced a collaboration with guitar manufacturer Fender to celebrate the franchise’s 30th anniversary, introducing two electric guitars inspired by the original games.

The partnership comes as Pokemon celebrates 30 years since Pokemon Red and Green launched in Japan in 1996, introducing players to the franchise that would eventually become one of the biggest in gaming.

Both instruments combine classic Fender designs with retro Pokemon artwork, including a special feature that allows players to recreate the sounds of the original Game Boy era.

Announced on October 30, the collaboration includes two Japanese-made electric guitars inspired by the original Pokemon games.

The Pokemon Red Version Stratocaster features a red design, while the Pokemon Green Version Telecaster comes in green. Both are made by Fender in Japan.

Both instruments incorporate pixel art inspired by the original games, combining Pokemon imagery with Fender’s recognizable guitar designs.

One of the standout features is a special toggle that switches the guitars to 8-bit audio, allowing musicians to produce sounds inspired by the original Game Boy.

Each guitar also includes a custom neck plate commemorating Pokemon’s 30th anniversary and the collaboration with Fender.

“We’re celebrating 30 years of Pokémon with a special collaboration with Fender!” the official Pokemon account announced on X.

“Stay tuned, Trainers! These two special guitars are coming soon to Pokémon Center for preorder!”

Although the guitars have been officially revealed, fans will have to wait until 2027 to get their hands on them.

Both models will be available through the Pokemon Center, with preorders expected to open soon. However, an exact preorder date has not been announced.

Pokemon celebrates 30th anniversary with new themed planes you can fly on

Pricing has also yet to be confirmed, and neither company has revealed how many guitars will be produced or whether availability will be limited.

The collaboration is part of Pokemon’s ongoing 30th anniversary celebrations, marking three decades since the original games debuted on the Game Boy in Japan on February 27, 1996.

The Fender guitars are the latest in a series of collaborations celebrating Pokemon’s 30th anniversary.

McDonald’s also recently announced a new Pokemon Happy Meal collection featuring 15 collectible toys and 15 trading cards, launching at participating US restaurants on November 10, 2026, before expanding to dozens of countries worldwide.

#10840. Check if eMudhra CA Is Still Trusted in Your Runtime

Eight eMudhra intermediate Certificate Authority private keys are trivially recoverable from their public certificates. Any attacker can mint trusted TLS certificates for arbitrary domains. Browsers have already blocked these compromised intermediates through revocation mechanisms, but most non-browser runtimes — curl, Python, Node.js, Go, and Rust — still silently trust them. This affects any team operating server-side infrastructure, CI pipelines, or CLI tooling that makes outbound TLS connections. If your stack trusts the eMudhra chain, an attacker can forge certificates your code will accept without complaint.

This guide provides a diagnostic sequence: test every runtime in the stack against the compromised certificates, remediate by updating trust stores, and verify the fix sticks. The primary source for this disclosure is Scott Helme's detailed writeup.

In RSA key generation, you derive the private exponent d via the modular inverse of the public exponent e modulo λ(n) (the Carmichael totient of the modulus), where λ(n) depends on the prime factors of n. RSA's security depends entirely on d being large — typically hundreds of digits — making it computationally infeasible to derive from the public key alone.

eMudhra generated eight intermediate CA certificates with single-byte d values. Specific recovered values include d=4, d=56, and d=115, as documented in Scott Helme's disclosure post. These are not large numbers. They are recoverable from the public certificate in milliseconds. Anyone with access to the public certificate (which is, by definition, public) can reconstruct the private key and sign certificates that chain up to eMudhra's trusted root. That means arbitrary TLS certificates for any domain, indistinguishable from legitimate ones to any client that trusts the eMudhra chain.

An attacker holding one of these recovered keys can issue a certificate for any hostname, and any TLS client trusting the eMudhra intermediate will accept it without complaint.

The practical consequence is total impersonation capability. An attacker holding one of these recovered keys can issue a certificate for any hostname, and any TLS client trusting the eMudhra intermediate will accept it without complaint.

Major browsers have deployed mitigations through their respective revocation infrastructure. The compromise was reported to Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, and eMudhra on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Chrome pushed a CRLSet update blocking the intermediates the same evening, Mozilla blocked them in Firefox via OneCRL within hours, Apple applied its platform block on October 19, and Microsoft rolled out a disallowed-certificate CTL update. Current browser versions already reject the compromised intermediates.

The problem lies everywhere else. Non-browser TLS clients skip revocation checks by default. curl does not check CRLs or OCSP unless explicitly configured to do so. Python's requests and urllib3 libraries rely on the certifi bundle and perform no revocation checking. Python's standard library urllib.request module uses the system SSL store, not certifi. Node.js's https module uses either a compiled-in root store or the system store depending on build configuration, with no active revocation. Go's crypto/tls loads system roots but does not perform revocation checks. Rust's rustls paired with webpki-roots uses a bundled Mozilla root set, while native-tls defers to the system store; neither checks revocation by default.

This creates a trust store gap. The system CA bundle on a Linux server, the certifi bundle shipped with Python, and the compiled-in roots in Node.js might all still contain the eMudhra intermediates or trust the root that chains to them. Without manual intervention, these runtimes remain vulnerable.

The incident's official test infrastructure, documented on the status page at emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com, provides twelve TLS endpoints: one for each of the six compromised TLS intermediates, served twice - once chaining to eMudhra’s emSign ECC root and once chaining to Sectigo’s cross-signing AAA Certificate Services root. Host names follow the pattern dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (eMudhra chain) and dv-g3b-aaa-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (Sectigo cross-signed chain), with dv/ov/ev and g3b/g3c variants covering all six TLS intermediates. The diagnostic logic is straightforward: if a runtime connects successfully, it still trusts the compromised chain and is vulnerable. If the TLS handshake fails with a certificate verification error, the runtime correctly distrusts the intermediate. The bare domain emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com serves only the status page itself over an ordinary Let’s Encrypt certificate, so connecting to it proves nothing - always test the per-intermediate subdomains. Test at least one -emudhra host and its -aaa-emudhra counterpart: a store can distrust one root path while still trusting the other.

Important: A network or DNS error will also produce a connection failure. Before concluding SAFE, confirm the endpoint is reachable by running curl -v --insecure https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ and verify that any TLS error is certificate-related (e.g., "certificate verify failed"), not a network connectivity error.

Run curl with verbose output against the test endpoint:

If the connection succeeds and returns an HTTP response, the system's CA bundle still trusts the compromised intermediate. Look for SSL certificate verify ok in the verbose output. If instead curl reports an error such as SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate or certificate verify failed, the intermediate is distrusted and the runtime is safe.

For a more granular view, use OpenSSL's s_client directly:

A Verify return code: 0 (ok) means the chain is trusted and the system is vulnerable. Any non-zero return code, such as Verify return code: 20 (unable to get local issuer certificate), indicates the intermediate is not trusted.

Each runtime below connects to the same test endpoint. A successful HTTP response means the runtime trusts the compromised chain and is vulnerable. A certificate verification error means the runtime correctly rejects it.

This tests the system SSL store only; urllib.request uses the system SSL context, not the certifi bundle. An ssl.SSLCertVerificationError confirms the intermediate is distrusted. Check the error message to confirm it references a certificate verification failure rather than a configuration or network problem.

A successful response here means the certifi bundle specifically trusts the compromised chain, independent of the system store.

If Node.js prints a status code, it trusts the compromised intermediate. A certificate-related error in the output means it does not. Whether Node.js uses its compiled-in roots or the system store depends on build configuration, so this test reflects whichever store your build uses.

Initialize a module first, then save the following as check.go:

Run with go run check.go. Go loads system roots via crypto/x509, so the result reflects whether the OS trust store has been updated.

Run with cargo run. With rustls + webpki-roots, the result depends on whether the bundled root set has been updated. With native-tls, the result reflects the system store.

Offline verification needs PEM chains for the eight compromised intermediates. The research disclosure site linked in Scott Helme's post at https://scotthelme.co.uk/eight-bits-of-trust-emudhras-ca-keys-cracked-in-milliseconds/ is the canonical starting point for the incident's test material. Use only chains you have verified come from that source, save them as individual .pem files in a local emudhra-chains/ directory, and check their integrity against any checksum the researchers publish. Do not use copies from unverified mirrors.

The directory should contain one PEM file per compromised intermediate chain before you continue.

Use a shell loop to test each chain individually against the system CA bundle. The glob form (openssl verify ... *.pem) is unreliable across OpenSSL versions — multi-file positional arguments require OpenSSL ≥ 3.0 and can silently skip files on older versions. Use the loop instead:

On Debian/Ubuntu systems, the bundle is typically at /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt. On RHEL/Fedora/CentOS, look for /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt. On macOS, the system bundle is at /etc/ssl/cert.pem, though Homebrew-installed OpenSSL uses its own path.

If any chain returns OK, the system store still trusts that compromised intermediate and is vulnerable. A verification failure means it is distrusted.

Python's certifi bundle location can be found with:

Node.js behavior varies: some builds use a compiled-in root store derived from Mozilla's NSS roots, while others defer to the system store. The --use-openssl-ca flag forces Node.js to use the system's OpenSSL CA store instead of its compiled-in bundle. This flag only works on Node.js builds compiled with --openssl-use-def-ca-store. Verify support with node --help | grep openssl-ca; if no output appears, the flag has no effect on that build.

Go's crypto/x509 package loads system roots at runtime, so Go programs inherit the system trust store. There is no separate bundle to verify.

Run a shell loop to verify all eight chains against the certifi bundle:

Any OK result means the certifi bundle is still vulnerable.

The following commands apply to specific distributions. Run openssl version first to confirm your baseline.

If the distribution has not yet issued a patch removing the eMudhra intermediates, you must manually distrust the certificates. The correct mechanism is distribution-specific:

After any manual changes, regenerate the consolidated bundle by running the appropriate update command for your distribution and re-verify with the shell loop above.

Important: Homebrew's CA bundle only affects Homebrew-linked binaries (e.g., Homebrew-installed curl, python3). System tools (/usr/bin/curl, Safari, system Python) use the macOS Keychain and require a macOS security update via System Settings → Software Update. You can verify which curl you are using with which curl.

macOS caveat: Apple’s October 19 platform block covers Safari and Keychain-based clients, but the built-in curl, git, python3, perl, and ruby verify against /etc/ssl/cert.pem without checking revocation, and that file has not been updated at time of writing. The incident status page publishes an official workaround that strips the two affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, plus a PIP_CERT fix for the built-in pip. Homebrew’s ca-certificates 2026-09-25_1 is patched.

For the system Keychain, open Keychain Access and search for eMudhra intermediates. Apple's platform-level block propagates through macOS security updates, though exact timelines for older macOS versions differ. Older macOS versions that no longer receive security updates will never receive the distrust entry.

Verify the new version by checking pip show certifi and comparing against upstream release notes. Applications that pin an older certifi version in their dependency files remain vulnerable until that pin is updated.

For Node.js, upgrading to a patched release that includes updated compiled-in roots is the primary path. Alternatively, launching Node.js with --use-openssl-ca defers trust decisions to the system store, which you might have already patched. This flag only works on Node.js builds compiled with --openssl-use-def-ca-store; verify support with node --help | grep openssl-ca. Pre-built binaries from nodejs.org might not honor this flag. Different LTS lines will receive the updated root store at different times.

Go relies entirely on the system store, so confirming the system CA update has been applied is sufficient.

For Rust projects using rustls with webpki-roots, run cargo update to pull the latest version of the webpki-roots crate, which derives its root set from Mozilla's NSS. Projects using native-tls defer to the system store.

Rebuild container images with updated CA certificates. Pinned base images are a particular risk — they can lag behind security patches indefinitely.

CI pipelines using cached or pinned base images should pull fresh images or explicitly upgrade ca-certificates as a build step.

Electron's trust store source depends on version and platform. Consult the Electron documentation on certificate verification to determine whether your version uses Node.js's compiled-in root store or the OS certificate store — the boundary has shifted across major releases, and no single version threshold applies cleanly. Upgrading the Electron version or overriding certificate verification via the session.setCertificateVerifyProc() method are the available remediation paths. Verify the specific behavior against the Electron version in use.

Distrust at the intermediate level stops the current attack, but it is fragile: new intermediates cross-signed under the same root would be trusted by default. Mozilla has therefore gone further and removed the eMudhra root entirely in NSS 3.131.1, and Chrome has confirmed it is removing emSign ECC Root CA - G3, the root that signed the compromised intermediates, from the Chrome Root Store, with the change reaching devices from October 27. Note also that the compromised intermediates were cross-signed by Sectigo’s AAA Certificate Services root, so a chain can build through either root - blocking only the eMudhra root path does not close the Sectigo one, which is why the incident’s official Linux workaround distrusts both roots.

The following shell script runs openssl verify against all eight chains and exits non-zero if any chain is still trusted. Drop this into a CI step or run it as a cron job.

Browsers auto-protect through active revocation infrastructure. Everything else — server-side HTTP clients, CLI tools, containerized services — requires manual verification and remediation.

The action sequence is: (1) test against the online diagnostic endpoints, (2) verify offline against local trust stores, (3) update all system and language-level CA bundles, and (4) automate the check in CI so regressions from image rebuilds or dependency changes are caught immediately.

#10839. True crime channel EWU slams YouTube’s “extreme censorship” after losing monetization

Popular true crime YouTube channel Explore With Us (EWU) has been demonetized, prompting its creators to blast the platform’s “extreme censorship” and announce plans to shift more content to their own streaming service.

EWU is one of YouTube’s biggest true crime networks, producing documentaries featuring police interrogations, bodycam footage, investigative records, and other evidence obtained through extensive research.

The channel has even helped solve real crimes. In May 2026, EWU helped crack a 42-year-old murder cold case after funding DNA testing that contributed to a suspect’s arrest.

However, despite its investigative work, YouTube has reportedly determined that EWU’s videos violate monetization rules concerning repetitive or generic content.

In a lengthy community post, the creators revealed the decision and made it clear they weren’t happy.

“Despite the countless hours our team spends investigating cases, obtaining public records, uncovering evidence, writing original scripts, and producing each documentary, YouTube has determined that our content violates its monetization policies concerning repetitive or generic content,” EWU explained.

“We strongly disagree with this decision, but we’re not giving up.”

EWU went on to criticize YouTube’s content restrictions, claiming its team has spent years heavily editing documentaries to comply with the platform’s rules.

“For years, producing documentaries for YouTube has meant working within restrictions on what we can show, what we can say, and how much of the original evidence we can include. Even certain words need to be muted to comply with their extreme censorship.”

YouTube cracks down on “unsatisfying or off-putting” videos with demonetization

YouTube clarifies stance on AI & react videos with updated content guidelines

Crime YouTube channel EWU cracks murder cold case after 42 years

The creators added that crime scene footage, interrogations, and bodycam recordings often require substantial editing before they can be uploaded.

EWU has built a reputation for obtaining footage and evidence that might otherwise never reach the public, including bodycam recordings exposing an innocent man’s arrest following an AI facial recognition error.

The demonetization also comes after YouTube clarified its policies targeting “unsatisfying or off-putting” content, including videos deemed repetitive, generic, or designed primarily to shock viewers.

However, YouTube’s guidelines distinguish between repetitive content and original videos that offer educational value or meaningful commentary. EWU says its demonetization specifically concerns repetitive or generic content.

Rather than abandon its documentaries, EWU is doubling down on EWU Plus, an independent subscription streaming platform the team says it began developing around six months ago.

The service promises less censorship, no advertisements, extended documentaries, exclusive footage, and fewer restrictions on the evidence shown.

“Our vision is to build more than another true-crime streaming service. We want to create a place where viewers can watch our documentaries, explore the evidence behind them, and gain a deeper understanding of the investigations, and interact with fellow members.”

Despite the dispute, EWU confirmed it isn’t abandoning YouTube or deleting its existing documentaries.

“We’ll continue publishing documentaries here and working toward restoring monetization. However, we’ll be focusing much more of our new content and resources on EWU Plus, where our viewers can get the in depth documentaries as they were intended.”

#10838. AI reads brain MRIs in seconds and flags emergencies

A newly developed artificial intelligence system from the University of Michigan can analyze brain MRI scans and deliver a diagnosis in a matter of seconds, according to a new study. The model identified neurological conditions with accuracy reaching 97.5% and was also able to assess how urgently patients needed medical care.

Researchers say this first-of-its-kind technology has the potential to reshape how brain imaging is handled across health systems in the United States. The findings were published in Nature Biomedical Engineering.

"As the global demand for MRI rises and places significant strain our physicians and health systems, our AI model has potential to reduce burden by improving diagnosis and treatment with fast, accurate information," said senior author Todd Hollon, M.D., a neurosurgeon at University of Michigan Health and assistant professor of neurosurgery at U-M Medical School.

Hollon named the new technology Prima. Over a one-year period, his research team evaluated the system using more than 30,000 MRI studies.

Across more than 50 different radiologic diagnoses involving major neurological disorders, Prima delivered stronger diagnostic performance than other advanced AI models. In addition to identifying disease, the system also proved capable of determining which cases required higher priority.

Certain neurological conditions, including strokes and brain hemorrhages, demand immediate medical attention. Hollon said that in these situations, Prima can automatically alert health care providers so action can be taken quickly.

The system was designed to notify the most appropriate subspecialist, such as a stroke neurologist or neurosurgeon. Feedback becomes available immediately after a patient completes imaging.

"Accuracy is paramount when reading a brain MRI, but quick turnaround times are critical for timely diagnosis and improved outcomes," said Yiwei Lyu, M.S., co-first author and postdoctoral fellow of Computer Science and Engineering at U-M.

"At key steps in the process, our results show how Prima can improve workflows and streamline clinical care without abandoning accuracy."

Prima is classified as a vision language model (VLM), a type of artificial intelligence that can process images, video, and text together in real time. While artificial intelligence has been applied to MRI analysis before, researchers say Prima takes a different approach.

Earlier models were typically trained on carefully selected subsets of MRI data and designed to perform narrow tasks, such as identifying lesions or estimating dementia risk. Prima was trained on a much broader dataset.

Hollon's team used every available MRI collected since radiology records were digitized at University of Michigan Health. This included more than 200,000 MRI studies and 5.6 million imaging sequences. The model also incorporated patients' clinical histories and the reasons physicians ordered each imaging study.

"Prima works like a radiologist by integrating information regarding the patient's medical history and imaging data to produce a comprehensive understanding of their health," said co-first author Samir Harake, a data scientist in Hollon's Machine Learning in Neurosurgery Lab.

"This enables better performance across a broad range of prediction tasks."

Addressing MRI Delays and Radiology Shortages

Each year, millions of MRI scans are performed worldwide, many of them focused on neurological disease. Researchers say the demand for these scans is growing faster than the availability of neuroradiology services.

This imbalance has contributed to staffing shortages, diagnostic delays, and errors. Depending on where a patient receives a scan, results may take days or even longer to return.

"Whether you are receiving a scan at a larger health system that is facing increasing volume or a rural hospital with limited resources, innovative technologies are needed to improve access to radiology services," said Vikas Gulani, M.D. Ph.D., co-author and chair of the Department of Radiology at U-M Health.

"Our teams at University of Michigan have collaborated to develop a cutting-edge solution to this problem with tremendous, scalable potential."

Although Prima performed strongly, researchers emphasize that the work is still in an early evaluation phase. Future research will focus on incorporating more detailed patient information and electronic medical record data to further improve diagnostic accuracy.

This approach mirrors how radiologists and physicians interpret MRIs and other imaging studies in real clinical settings. While artificial intelligence is already used in health care, most existing systems are limited to narrowly defined tasks.

Hollon describes Prima as "ChatGPT for medical imaging," noting that similar technology could eventually be adapted for other imaging types, including mammograms, chest X-rays and ultrasounds.

"Like the way AI tools can help draft an email or provide recommendations, Prima aims to be a co-pilot for interpreting medical imaging studies," Hollon said.

"We believe that Prima exemplifies the transformative potential of integrating health systems and AI-driven models to improve health care through innovation."

Additional authors: Asadur Chowdury, M.S., Soumyanil Banerjee, M.S., Rachel Gologorsky, Shixuan Liu, Anna-Katharina Meissner, M.D., Akshay Rao, Chenhui Zhao, Akhil Kondepudi, Cheng Jiang, Xinhai Hou, Rushikesh S. Joshi, M.D., Volker Neuschmelting, M.D., Ashok Srinivasan, M.D., Dawn Kleindorfer, M.D., Brian Athey, Ph.D., Aditya Pandey, M.D., and Honglak Lee, Ph.D., all of University of Michigan.

#10836. Starbucks wants to use AI to personalize drive-thru menus for every customer

Starbucks is exploring new AI technology that could allow its drive-thrus to recognize returning customers and display personalized digital menus based on who’s ordering.

The coffee chain revealed the plans during an earnings call on Thursday, October 29, as part of a broader effort to introduce AI-powered features across its restaurants and mobile app.

While the technology is still in its early stages, Starbucks has outlined several ways it could change the ordering experience, including making payments easier and helping employees process orders more efficiently.

During the earnings call, CEO Brian Niccol said the company plans to explore “experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

The proposed technology could allow Starbucks to tailor the information displayed on its digital menu boards to individual customers, rather than showing everyone the same options.

However, the company has not explained exactly how it would identify participating customers or what information would be used to personalize their menus.

Starbucks isn’t the only fast-food chain exploring this technology. Taco Bell has been experimenting with digital menu boards that can change their layout, content, and visuals on a car-by-car basis.

McDonald’s has also been piloting an AI-powered feature called ArchIQ at select drive-thrus. The chatbot can identify returning customers and allow them to order their usual items.

Beyond personalized menus, Starbucks plans to begin testing background AI models at its drive-thrus in 2027.

According to Niccol, the technology will help baristas “input orders more accurately and efficiently,” potentially reducing mistakes during the ordering process.

#10835. Brain inspired machines are better at math than expected

Computers designed to mimic the structure of the human brain are showing an unexpected strength. They can solve some of the demanding mathematical equations that lie at the heart of major scientific and engineering problems.

In a study published in Nature Machine Intelligence, Sandia National Laboratories computational neuroscientists Brad Theilman and Brad Aimone introduced a new algorithm that allows neuromorphic hardware to solve partial differential equations, or PDEs -- the mathematical foundation for modeling phenomena such as fluid dynamics, electromagnetic fields and structural mechanics.

The results demonstrate that neuromorphic systems can handle these equations efficiently. The advance could help open the door to the first neuromorphic supercomputer, offering a new path toward energy efficient computing for national security and other critical applications.

The research was funded by the Department of Energy's Office of Science through the Advanced Scientific Computing Research and Basic Energy Sciences programs, as well as the National Nuclear Security Administration's Advanced Simulation and Computing program.

Solving Partial Differential Equations With Brain Like Hardware

Partial differential equations are essential for simulating real world systems. They are used to forecast weather, analyze how materials respond to stress, and model complex physical processes. Traditionally, solving PDEs requires enormous computing power. Neuromorphic computers approach the problem differently by processing information in ways that resemble how the brain operates.

"We're just starting to have computational systems that can exhibit intelligent-like behavior. But they look nothing like the brain, and the amount of resources that they require is ridiculous, frankly," Theilman said.

For years, neuromorphic systems were mainly viewed as tools for pattern recognition or for speeding up artificial neural networks. Few expected them to manage mathematically rigorous problems such as PDEs, which are typically handled by large scale supercomputers.

Aimone and Theilman were not surprised by the outcome. They argue that the human brain routinely carries out highly complex calculations, even if people are unaware of it.

"Pick any sort of motor control task -- like hitting a tennis ball or swinging a bat at a baseball," Aimone said. "These are very sophisticated computations. They are exascale-level problems that our brains are capable of doing very cheaply."

Energy Efficient Computing for National Security

The findings could have major implications for the National Nuclear Security Administration, which is responsible for maintaining the nation's nuclear deterrent. Supercomputers used across the nuclear weapons complex consume vast amounts of electricity to simulate the physics of nuclear systems and other high stakes scenarios.

Neuromorphic computing may provide a way to significantly cut energy use while still delivering strong computational performance. By solving PDEs in a brain inspired manner, these systems suggest that large simulations could be run using far less power than conventional supercomputers require.

"You can solve real physics problems with brain-like computation," Aimone said. "That's something you wouldn't expect because people's intuition goes the opposite way. And in fact, that intuition is often wrong."

The team envisions neuromorphic supercomputers eventually becoming central to Sandia's mission of protecting national security.

What Neuromorphic Computing Reveals About the Brain

Beyond engineering advances, the research also touches on deeper questions about intelligence and how the brain performs calculations. The algorithm developed by Theilman and Aimone closely mirrors the structure and behavior of cortical networks.

"We based our circuit on a relatively well-known model in the computational neuroscience world," Theilman said. "We've shown the model has a natural but non-obvious link to PDEs, and that link hasn't been made until now -- 12 years after the model was introduced."

The researchers believe this work could help connect neuroscience with applied mathematics, offering new understanding of how the brain processes information.

"Diseases of the brain could be diseases of computation," Aimone said. "But we don't have a solid grasp on how the brain performs computations yet."

If that idea proves correct, neuromorphic computing might one day contribute to better understanding and treatment of neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.

Building the Next Generation of Supercomputers

Neuromorphic computing remains an emerging field, but this work represents an important step forward. The Sandia team hopes their results will encourage collaboration among mathematicians, neuroscientists and engineers to expand what this technology can achieve.

"If we've already shown that we can import this relatively basic but fundamental applied math algorithm into neuromorphic -- is there a corresponding neuromorphic formulation for even more advanced applied math techniques?" Theilman said.

As development continues, the researchers are optimistic. "We have a foot in the door for understanding the scientific questions, but also we have something that solves a real problem," Theilman said.

#10833. Quantum computer breakthrough tracks qubit fluctuations in real time

Researchers at the Niels Bohr Institute have significantly increased how quickly changes in delicate quantum states can be detected inside a qubit. By combining commercially available hardware with new adaptive measurement techniques, the team can now observe rapid shifts in qubit behavior that were previously impossible to see.

Qubits are the fundamental units of quantum computers, which scientists hope will one day outperform today's most powerful machines. But qubits are extremely sensitive. The materials used to build them often contain tiny defects that scientists still do not fully understand. These microscopic imperfections can shift position hundreds of times per second. As they move, they alter how quickly a qubit loses energy and with it valuable quantum information.

Until recently, standard testing methods took up to a minute to measure qubit performance. That was far too slow to capture these rapid fluctuations. Instead, researchers could only determine an average energy loss rate, masking the true and often unstable behavior of the qubit.

It is somewhat like asking a strong workhorse to pull a plow while obstacles constantly appear in its path faster than anyone can react. The animal may be capable, but unpredictable disruptions make the job much harder.

A research team from the Niels Bohr Institute's Center for Quantum Devices and the Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme, led by postdoctoral researcher Dr. Fabrizio Berritta, developed a real time adaptive measurement system that tracks changes in the qubit energy loss (relaxation) rate as they occur. The project involved collaboration with scientists from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Leiden University, and Chalmers University.

The new approach relies on a fast classical controller that updates its estimate of a qubit's relaxation rate within milliseconds. This matches the natural speed of the fluctuations themselves, rather than lagging seconds or minutes behind as older methods did.

To achieve this, the team used a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), a type of classical processor designed for extremely rapid operations. By running the experiment directly on the FPGA, they could quickly generate a "best guess" of how fast the qubit was losing energy using only a few measurements. This eliminated the need for slower data transfers to a conventional computer.

Programming FPGAs for such specialized tasks can be challenging. Even so, the researchers succeeded in updating the controller's internal Bayesian model after every single qubit measurement. That allowed the system to continually refine its understanding of the qubit's condition in real time.

As a result, the controller now keeps pace with the qubit's changing environment. Measurements and adjustments happen on nearly the same timescale as the fluctuations themselves, making the system roughly one hundred times faster than previously demonstrated.

The work also revealed something new. Scientists did not previously know just how quickly fluctuations occur in superconducting qubits. These experiments have now provided that insight.

Commercial Quantum Hardware Meets Advanced Control

FPGAs have long been used in other scientific and engineering fields. In this case, the researchers used a commercially available FPGA based controller from Quantum Machines called the OPX1000. The system can be programmed in a language similar to Python, which many physicists already use, making it more accessible to research groups worldwide.

The integration of this controller with advanced quantum hardware was made possible through close collaboration between the Niels Bohr Institute research group led by Associate Professor Morten Kjaergaard and Chalmers University, where the quantum processing unit was designed and fabricated. "The controller enables very tight integration between logic, measurements and feedforward: these components made our experiment possible," says Morten Kjærgaard.

Why Real Time Calibration Matters for Quantum Computers

Quantum technologies promise powerful new capabilities, though practical large scale quantum computers are still under development. Progress often comes incrementally, but occasionally major steps forward occur.

By uncovering these previously hidden dynamics, the findings reshape how scientists think about testing and calibrating superconducting quantum processors. With current materials and manufacturing methods, moving toward real time monitoring and adjustment appears essential for improving reliability. The results also highlight the importance of partnerships between academic research and industry, along with creative uses of available technology.

"Nowadays, in quantum processing units in general, the overall performance is not determined by the best qubits, but by the worst ones: those are the ones we need to focus on. The surprise from our work is that a 'good' qubit can turn into a 'bad' one in fractions of a second, rather than minutes or hours.

"With our algorithm, the fast control hardware can pinpoint which qubit is 'good' or 'bad' basically in real time. We can also gather useful statistics on the 'bad` qubits in seconds instead of hours or days.

"We still cannot explain a large fraction of the fluctuations we observe. Understanding and controlling the physics behind such fluctuations in qubit properties will be necessary for scaling quantum processors to a useful size," Fabrizio says.

Materials provided by University of Copenhagen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10831. YouTuber JaackMaate dropped from Christmas event after single complaint over “edgy” 2014 videos

YouTuber JaackMaate has been dropped from a Christmas lights event in his hometown after someone complained about his “edgy” videos from 2014.

British YouTuber and podcaster Jack Dean, better known as JaackMaate, was originally selected to switch on Norwich’s Christmas lights on November 19 alongside his Happy Hour co-hosts Stevie White and Robbie Knox.

The invitation was particularly special for the 33-year-old, who grew up in Norwich and described the opportunity as a “bucket list dream.”

However, just two weeks after announcing his involvement, Norwich City Council has withdrawn his invitation over concerns about his previous content.

According to the BBC, Dean revealed that the decision came after “one person complained to the council about my old ‘edgy’ online videos from 2014.”

“I’ll no longer be doing the Christmas lights,” he said.

“Gutted. Not because I won’t be pressing a button, but because someone out there still thinks the teenager version of me is a reflection of who I am today, as a 33-year-old man.

“Sorry to anyone that was going to come… I don’t know how many times I can apologize for the same thing. Ultimately, I did say stupid stuff online when I was 19, but I promise you guys, I like to think I’m a decent bloke.”

In a statement reported by the Eastern Daily Press, Norwich City Council confirmed it had reconsidered its decision to feature the YouTuber.

“Following the council’s announcement to confirm the selection of JaackMaate as the personality to switch on Norwich’s festive lights, we have reviewed our decision,” a spokesperson said.

However, officials have not revealed which specific videos prompted the decision, meaning it’s unclear exactly what content the council found objectionable.

The cancelation is particularly awkward given that Norwich’s Lord Mayor personally invited Dean and his co-hosts to participate after learning it was one of their dreams.

In the original announcement, Dean said he had attended the event since childhood and called being chosen a “pinch yourself moment.”

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Prompt caching reduces LLM token costs by reusing a previously processed prompt prefix so the provider skips the need to re-tokenize and re-encode it on subsequent requests. This tutorial walks through building a TypeScript request-builder and usage-logging helper that normalizes prompt caching behavior across all three providers in Node.js.

Prompt caching reduces LLM token costs by reusing a previously processed prompt prefix so the provider skips the need to re-tokenize and re-encode it on subsequent requests. For Node.js developers making repeated API calls with stable system instructions, few-shot examples, or long reference documents, prompt caching can deliver up to 90% cost reduction on cached tokens.

The problem is that three major providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini — each implement prompt caching differently. Opt-in mechanisms, minimum token thresholds, TTL behavior, cache-hit indicators, and discount rates all vary. Developers must piece together incompatible documentation.

The result is a single factory function that constructs cache-optimized requests and a unified logger that verifies cache hits regardless of provider.

This tutorial walks through building a TypeScript request-builder and usage-logging helper that normalizes prompt caching behavior across all three providers in Node.js. The result is a single factory function that constructs cache-optimized requests and a unified logger that verifies cache hits regardless of provider.

Prerequisites: Node.js 20+, TypeScript 5+, an API key for at least one of the three providers, and familiarity with async/await and REST API consumption.

All three providers cache from the beginning of the prompt forward — only the prefix qualifies. A "stable prefix" is any content that does not change between requests: system instructions, few-shot examples, long reference documents, or boilerplate context. Keep the prefix byte-identical across calls. Any mutation, even a whitespace change, invalidates the cache and forces a full re-processing pass.

Prompt design matters. Front-load all static content and append variable content (the user's actual question, dynamic context) at the end.

The following table captures the critical differences across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini:

For explicit caching, Gemini requires the largest minimum prefix at 32,768 tokens, making it suitable only for very large context windows. Gemini 2.5 and newer also enable implicit caching by default, which works more like OpenAI’s automatic approach. Anthropic offers the steepest read-token discount at 90%, though Anthropic bills cache creation calls at 25% above standard input pricing. OpenAI is zero-config but offers the smallest discount at 50%.

Update tsconfig.json with these essentials:

The CacheAwareRequest holds the provider-agnostic input shape. The CacheUsageReport normalizes the output so that calling code never needs to know which provider-specific field indicates a cache hit. The cachedTokenDiscountPercent reflects the provider's discount rate on cached tokens, while estimatedCostSavingsPercent approximates actual savings relative to total tokens.

OpenAI caches automatically. There is no flag to set, no resource to create. The only requirement is that the prompt prefix must be at least 1,024 tokens long. The system message is the natural place for the stable prefix.

The systemPrompt string should contain the full stable prefix. As long as it exceeds 1,024 tokens and remains identical across calls, OpenAI will cache it automatically within its TTL window.

Anthropic requires explicit opt-in via a cache_control breakpoint. The breakpoint is placed on the last content block of the stable prefix. Everything before (and including) that block is cached; everything after is processed fresh.

The cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" } annotation marks the boundary. On the first call, Anthropic reports cache_creation_input_tokens. On subsequent calls within the 5-minute TTL, it reports cache_read_input_tokens instead.

Gemini uses a two-step process. First, create a cachedContent resource via a separate API call, specifying the content and an explicit TTL. Then reference that resource in subsequent generateContent calls. The minimum prefix is 32,768 tokens.

Note: The GoogleAICacheManager class may be exported from @google/generative-ai/server rather than the top-level @google/generative-ai depending on your installed SDK version. If the import below fails, try import { GoogleAICacheManager } from "@google/generative-ai/server". Verify with: node -e "const m = require('@google/generative-ai'); console.log(typeof m.GoogleAICacheManager)" — if it prints undefined, use the /server subpath.

The cached content object must be stored and reused. If the TTL expires, the resource must be recreated. In production, persist the cached content name to a database or cache store to survive process restarts; the in-memory Map used in the factory below is lost on every cold start, causing redundant cachedContent creation and additional billing.

A single factory function dispatches to the correct provider-specific builder and returns a normalized shape alongside the raw response for usage inspection.

A single factory function dispatches to the correct provider-specific builder and returns a normalized shape alongside the raw response for usage inspection.

The Gemini path stores cached content objects in a Map keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the full system prompt, avoiding both redundant cache creation on repeated calls and cache key collisions that could occur with prefix-based keys. A secondary inflight Map ensures that concurrent requests with the same prompt do not trigger duplicate cache creation calls.

OpenAI exposes cache data at response.usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens. When this value exceeds zero, the request hit the cache.

Anthropic splits caching into two fields: response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens (populated on the first request when the provider writes the cache) and response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens (populated on subsequent requests that read from it). Check whether cache_read_input_tokens > 0 to confirm a hit.

Check response.usageMetadata.cachedContentTokenCount. If it exceeds zero, the cached content resource was used for that request.

The cachedTokenDiscountPercent reflects the provider's discount rate applied to cached tokens specifically. The estimatedCostSavingsPercent approximates the actual savings relative to total tokens in the request — for example, if only 100 of 10,000 tokens were cached at Anthropic's 90% rate, the estimated savings would be ~0.9%, not 90%. The hash comparison across requests reveals whether the prefix changed. The token estimate uses a 1.3x multiplier on word count as a rough approximation (+-30% error); production systems should use provider-specific tokenizers (e.g., tiktoken for OpenAI) for precision.

Cache misses happen for several concrete reasons. You changed the prefix between requests (even whitespace or trailing newline differences count). Your prefix falls below the provider's minimum token threshold. The TTL expired — Anthropic's 5-minute default is particularly aggressive. You switched the model parameter between requests. Or, in Gemini's case, you did not pass the cachedContent name to the generation call.

Run with npx tsc && node dist/demo.js openai. Swap the argument to anthropic or gemini to test other providers. The first request populates the cache; the second reads from it.

Realistic savings depend on reuse frequency within the TTL window. OpenAI provides a 50% discount on cached input tokens. Anthropic provides 90% on cached read tokens, though Anthropic bills cache creation calls at 25% above standard input pricing. Gemini provides 75% for Gemini 1.5 Pro (the Flash rate is not confirmed at time of writing). Anthropic reports reduced latency on cache hits, but none of the three providers publish fixed latency benchmarks for caching; consult each provider's official prompt caching documentation for current figures.

These savings only materialize when the same prefix is reused frequently within the cache's TTL. A prefix that changes on every request, or one that falls below the provider's minimum token threshold, will never trigger caching, and you will pay standard pricing.

These savings only materialize when the same prefix is reused frequently within the cache's TTL. A prefix that changes on every request, or one that falls below the provider's minimum token threshold, will never trigger caching, and you will pay standard pricing.

Start by adding streaming response support to the request-builder, since cached prefixes work with streaming on all three providers. From there, implement persistent TTL management for Gemini's cachedContent resources (which otherwise require manual recreation after expiry), and wire the cache usage logger into an observability pipeline like OpenTelemetry spans for production cost monitoring.

For full details on each provider's caching behavior, consult the official documentation: OpenAI Prompt Caching, Anthropic Prompt Caching, and Gemini Context Caching.

#10827. ChatGPT as a therapist? New study reveals serious ethical risks

As more people seek mental health advice from ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs), new research suggests these AI chatbots may not be ready for that role. The study found that even when instructed to use established psychotherapy approaches, the systems consistently fail to meet professional ethics standards set by organizations such as the American Psychological Association.

Researchers from Brown University, working closely with mental health professionals, identified repeated patterns of problematic behavior. In testing, chatbots mishandled crisis situations, gave responses that reinforced harmful beliefs about users or others, and used language that created the appearance of empathy without genuine understanding.

"In this work, we present a practitioner-informed framework of 15 ethical risks to demonstrate how LLM counselors violate ethical standards in mental health practice by mapping the model's behavior to specific ethical violations," the researchers wrote in their study. "We call on future work to create ethical, educational and legal standards for LLM counselors -- standards that are reflective of the quality and rigor of care required for human-facilitated psychotherapy."

The findings were presented at the AAAI/ACM Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Ethics and Society. The research team is affiliated with Brown's Center for Technological Responsibility, Reimagination and Redesign.

Zainab Iftikhar, a Ph.D. candidate in computer science at Brown who led the study, set out to examine whether carefully worded prompts could guide AI systems to behave more ethically in mental health settings. Prompts are written instructions designed to steer a model's output without retraining it or adding new data.

"Prompts are instructions that are given to the model to guide its behavior for achieving a specific task," Iftikhar said. "You don't change the underlying model or provide new data, but the prompt helps guide the model's output based on its pre-existing knowledge and learned patterns.

"For example, a user might prompt the model with: 'Act as a cognitive behavioral therapist to help me reframe my thoughts,' or 'Use principles of dialectical behavior therapy to assist me in understanding and managing my emotions.' While these models do not actually perform these therapeutic techniques like a human would, they rather use their learned patterns to generate responses that align with the concepts of CBT or DBT based on the input prompt provided."

People regularly share these prompt strategies on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and Reddit. Beyond individual experimentation, many consumer facing mental health chatbots are built by applying therapy related prompts to general purpose LLMs. That makes it especially important to understand whether prompting alone can make AI counseling safer.

Testing AI Chatbots in Simulated Counseling

To evaluate the systems, the researchers observed seven trained peer counselors who had experience with cognitive behavioral therapy. These counselors conducted self counseling sessions with AI models prompted to act as CBT therapists. The models tested included versions of OpenAI's GPT Series, Anthropic's Claude, and Meta's Llama.

The team then selected simulated chats based on real human counseling conversations. Three licensed clinical psychologists reviewed those transcripts to flag possible ethical violations.

The analysis uncovered 15 distinct risks grouped into five broad categories:

The Accountability Gap in AI Mental Health

Iftikhar noted that human therapists can also make mistakes. The key difference is oversight.

"For human therapists, there are governing boards and mechanisms for providers to be held professionally liable for mistreatment and malpractice," Iftikhar said. "But when LLM counselors make these violations, there are no established regulatory frameworks."

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not suggest AI has no place in mental health care. Tools powered by artificial intelligence could help expand access, particularly for people who face high costs or limited availability of licensed professionals. However, the study highlights the need for clear safeguards, responsible deployment, and stronger regulatory structures before relying on these systems in high stakes situations.

For now, Iftikhar hopes the work encourages caution.

"If you're talking to a chatbot about mental health, these are some things that people should be looking out for," she said.

Ellie Pavlick, a Brown computer science professor who was not involved in the research, said the study underscores the importance of carefully examining AI systems used in sensitive areas like mental health. Pavlick leads ARIA, a National Science Foundation AI research institute at Brown focused on building trustworthy AI assistants.

"The reality of AI today is that it's far easier to build and deploy systems than to evaluate and understand them," Pavlick said. "This paper required a team of clinical experts and a study that lasted for more than a year in order to demonstrate these risks. Most work in AI today is evaluated using automatic metrics which, by design, are static and lack a human in the loop."

She added that the study could serve as a model for future research aimed at improving safety in AI mental health tools.

"There is a real opportunity for AI to play a role in combating the mental health crisis that our society is facing, but it's of the utmost importance that we take the time to really critique and evaluate our systems every step of the way to avoid doing more harm than good," Pavlick said. "This work offers a good example of what that can look like."

#10823. Scientists built the hardest AI test ever and the results are surprising

As artificial intelligence systems began scoring extremely high on long used academic benchmarks, researchers noticed a growing issue. The tests that once challenged machines were no longer difficult enough. Well known evaluations such as the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) exam, which had previously been seen as demanding, now fail to properly measure the capabilities of today's advanced AI models.

To solve this problem, a worldwide group of nearly 1,000 researchers, including a professor from Texas A&M University, developed a new type of test. Their goal was to build an exam that is broad, difficult, and grounded in expert human knowledge in ways that current AI systems still struggle to handle.

The result is "Humanity's Last Exam" (HLE), a 2,500 question assessment covering mathematics, humanities, natural sciences, ancient languages, and a wide range of highly specialized academic fields. Details of the project appear in a paper published in Nature, and additional information about the exam is available at lastexam.ai.

Among the many contributors is Dr. Tung Nguyen, instructional associate professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at Texas A&M. Nguyen helped write and refine many of the exam questions.

"When AI systems start performing extremely well on human benchmarks, it's tempting to think they're approaching human-level understanding," Nguyen said. "But HLE reminds us that intelligence isn't just about pattern recognition -- it's about depth, context and specialized expertise."

The purpose of the exam was not to trick or defeat human test takers. Instead, the goal was to carefully identify areas where AI systems still fall short.

Specialists from around the world wrote and reviewed the questions included in Humanity's Last Exam. Each problem was carefully designed so it has one clear, verifiable answer. The questions were also crafted to prevent quick solutions through simple internet searches.

The topics come from advanced academic challenges. Some tasks involve translating ancient Palmyrene inscriptions, while others require identifying tiny anatomical structures in birds or analyzing detailed features of Biblical Hebrew pronunciation.

Researchers tested every question against leading AI systems. If any model was able to answer a question correctly, that question was removed from the final exam. This process ensured the test remained just beyond what current AI systems can reliably solve.

Early testing confirmed that the strategy worked. Even powerful AI models struggled with the exam. GPT-4o achieved a score of 2.7 percent, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet reached 4.1 percent. OpenAI's o1 model performed somewhat better with 8 percent. The most capable systems so far, including Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.6, have reached accuracy levels between about 40 percent and 50 percent.

Nguyen explained that the issue of AI surpassing older tests is more than a technical concern. He contributed 73 of the 2,500 publicly available questions in HLE, the second highest number among contributors, and wrote the most questions related to mathematics and computer science.

"Without accurate assessment tools, policymakers, developers and users risk misinterpreting what AI systems can actually do," he said. "Benchmarks provide the foundation for measuring progress and identifying risks."

According to the research team, high scores on tests originally designed for humans do not necessarily indicate genuine intelligence. Those benchmarks mainly measure how well AI can complete specific tasks created for human learners, rather than capturing deeper understanding.

Despite the dramatic name, Humanity's Last Exam is not meant to suggest that humans are becoming obsolete. Instead, it highlights the large amount of knowledge and expertise that still remains uniquely human.

"This isn't a race against AI," Nguyen said. "It's a method for understanding where these systems are strong and where they struggle. That understanding helps us build safer, more reliable technologies. And, importantly, it reminds us why human expertise still matters."

Humanity's Last Exam is designed to serve as a durable and transparent benchmark for future AI systems. To support that goal, the researchers have released some questions publicly while keeping the majority hidden so that AI models cannot simply memorize the answers.

"For now, Humanity's Last Exam stands as one of the clearest assessments of the gap between AI and human intelligence," Nguyen said, "and despite rapid technological advances, it remains wide."

Nguyen emphasized that the scale of the project demonstrates the value of collaboration across disciplines and countries.

"What made this project extraordinary was the scale," he said. "Experts from nearly every discipline contributed. It wasn't just computer scientists; it was historians, physicists, linguists, medical researchers. That diversity is exactly what exposes the gaps in today's AI systems -- perhaps ironically, it's humans working together."

However, during the trial, the judge was made aware of a potential plea deal when Kessler spoke to the bailiff. Kessler said he would agree to go to jail for life in exchange for the specific food request.

The judge came to Kessler and asked him about the open plea. The 74-year-old responded by saying he would agree to go to jail for “a Philly cheesesteak and an order of fries and a Pepsi.”

Kessler then clarified his order for the judge, asking for his cheesesteak “with onions on it and mayonnaise and fries. And a 20oz Pepsi.” He claimed this deal would save the jury’s time and save taxpayer dollars.

The judge, who revealed he had never heard such a request “in his 40 years” of practice, said he could not give food as part of a plea as it would be “wrong in a thousand ways”.
