#10783. Think AI "knows" what it’s doing? Scientists say think again

These are everyday words people use to describe what goes on in the human mind. But when those same terms are applied to artificial intelligence, they can unintentionally make machines seem more human than they really are.

"We use mental verbs all the time in our daily lives, so it makes sense that we might also use them when we talk about machines -- it helps us relate to them," said Jo Mackiewicz, professor of English at Iowa State. "But at the same time, when we apply mental verbs to machines, there's also a risk of blurring the line between what humans and AI can do."

Mackiewicz and Jeanine Aune, a teaching professor of English and director of the advanced communication program at Iowa State, are part of a research team that studied how writers describe AI using human-like language. This type of wording, known as anthropomorphism, assigns human traits to non-human systems. Their study, "Anthropomorphizing Artificial Intelligence: A Corpus Study of Mental Verbs Used with AI and ChatGPT," was published in Technical Communication Quarterly.

The research team also included Matthew J. Baker, associate professor of linguistics at Brigham Young University, and Jordan Smith, assistant professor of English at the University of Northern Colorado. Both previously studied at Iowa State University.

Why Human-Like Language About AI Can Be Misleading

According to the researchers, using mental verbs to describe AI can create a false impression. Words such as "think," "know," "understand," and "want" suggest that a system has thoughts, intentions, or awareness. In reality, AI does not possess beliefs or feelings. It produces responses by analyzing patterns in data, not by forming ideas or making conscious decisions.

Mackiewicz and Aune also pointed out that this kind of language can overstate what AI is capable of. Phrases like "AI decided" or "ChatGPT knows" can make systems seem more independent or intelligent than they actually are. This can lead to unrealistic expectations about how reliable or capable AI is.

There is also a broader concern. When AI is described as if it has intentions, it can distract from the humans behind it. Developers, engineers, and organizations are responsible for how these systems are built and used.

"Certain anthropomorphic phrases may even stick in readers' minds and can potentially shape public perception of AI in unhelpful ways," Aune said.

How News Writers Actually Use AI Language

To better understand how often this kind of language appears, the researchers analyzed the News on the Web (NOW) corpus. This massive dataset contains more than 20 billion words from English-language news articles published in 20 countries.

They focused on how frequently mental verbs such as "learns," "means," and "knows" were used alongside terms like AI and ChatGPT.

Mental Verbs Are Less Common Than Expected

The study found that news writers do not frequently pair AI-related terms with mental verbs.

While anthropomorphism is common in everyday speech, it appears far less often in news writing. "Anthropomorphism has been shown to be common in everyday speech, but we found there's far less usage in news writing," Mackiewicz said.

Among the examples identified, the word "needs" appeared most often with AI, showing up 661 times. For ChatGPT, "knows" was the most frequent pairing, but it appeared only 32 times.

The researchers noted that editorial standards may play a role. Associated Press guidelines, which discourage attributing human emotions or traits to AI, could be influencing how journalists write about these technologies.

Context Matters More Than the Words Themselves

Even when mental verbs were used, they were not always anthropomorphic.

For instance, the word "needs" often described basic requirements rather than human-like qualities. Phrases such as "AI needs large amounts of data" or "AI needs some human assistance" are similar to how people describe non-human systems like cars or recipes. In these cases, the language does not imply that AI has thoughts or desires.

In other cases, "needs" was used to express what should be done, such as "AI needs to be trained" or "AI needs to be implemented." Aune explained that these examples were often written in passive voice, which shifts responsibility back to human actors rather than the technology itself.

The study also showed that not all uses of mental verbs are equal. Some phrases move closer to suggesting human-like qualities.

For example, statements like "AI needs to understand the real world" can imply expectations tied to human reasoning, ethics, or awareness. These uses go beyond simple descriptions and begin to suggest deeper capabilities.

"These instances showed that anthropomorphizing isn't all-or-nothing and instead exists on a spectrum," Aune said

Overall, the researchers found that anthropomorphism in news coverage is both less frequent and more nuanced than many might assume.

"Overall, our analysis shows that anthropomorphization of AI in news writing is far less common -- and far more nuanced -- than we might think," Mackiewicz said. "Even the instances that did anthropomorphize AI varied widely in strength."

The findings highlight the importance of context. Simply counting words is not enough to understand how language shapes meaning.

"For writers, this nuance matters: the language we choose shapes how readers understand AI systems, their capabilities and the humans responsible for them," Mackiewicz said.

The research team also emphasized that these insights can help professionals think more carefully about how they describe AI in their work.

"Our findings can help technical and professional communication practitioners reflect on how they think about AI technologies as tools in their writing process and how they write about AI," the research team wrote in the published study.

As AI continues to develop, the way people talk about it will remain important. Mackiewicz and Aune said writers will need to stay mindful of how word choices influence perception.

Looking ahead, the team suggested that future studies could explore how different words shape understanding and whether even rare uses of anthropomorphic language have a strong impact on how people view AI.

Materials provided by Iowa State University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

At a large company, the hard part of buying an AI brand mention tracking tool is procurement. IT asks about single sign-on, legal asks where the data sits, and the marketing team that wanted the tool waits weeks to log in. A pilot on one brand in one market looks cheap, then the other markets, the other teams and SSO arrive and the quote looks nothing like the trial.

That is why a generic "best tools" list helps enterprise buyers less than it should. All the tools below track how often ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI answers name your brand. What separates them at enterprise size is everything around the tracking: how many people can log in, how logins are controlled, whether the data can leave the tool and whether it copes with ten markets instead of one.

This guide compares six tools on those points. Peec AI ranks first because it combines unlimited users, enforceable SSO, source-level analysis and a published price ladder. The other five suit different buying situations.

AI brand mention tracking measures how often, where and how favourably AI engines name your brand when buyers ask category questions. A tool runs a fixed prompt set daily across engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode and Microsoft Copilot, then reports mention rate (visibility), position inside the answer, sentiment, share of voice against competitors and the sources each answer cited.

For an enterprise, the answers differ by engine, country and product line, and a single visibility number hides most of that. Similarweb's May 2026 figures put ChatGPT at 53.9% of AI chatbot web visits, Gemini at 27.9% and Claude at 9.2%, against roughly 76% for ChatGPT in June 2025. The question "what does AI say about us?" is now spread over at least three engines.

Access and identity. Ask how many users each plan allows, whether SSO is available and on which plan, and whether you can enforce it. Most tools put SSO on their top tier or a custom plan, so budget for an enterprise contract early.

Markets and brands. Check whether the price grows per country, language or brand. Ten markets multiply a prompt set quickly.

Data access. The data has to reach the reporting leadership already reads: CSV export, an API, a BI connector or an MCP server.

Source analysis. A mention rate shows where you stand. Source data shows why, by listing the pages each engine read. Without it you cannot tell whether you are missing because nobody writes about you or because your own pages are not picked up.

Prompt volume and engines. A hundred to a hundred and fifty prompts per brand and market is a realistic start. Check which engines each plan includes and which sit behind add-ons.

Cost at your real workload. Price the tool for the users, markets and prompts you will have in a year, not for the pilot.

Enterprise teams rarely run on the entry tier, so the tables below price two realistic workloads: about 150 prompts, and about 350 prompts on ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode with 15 users, both tracked daily on three engines. Price per prompt is the monthly price divided by the prompts the plan includes. Rankscale and AthenaHQ price by answers or credits instead, so Rankscale's rows use the answer volume the workload needs: 150 prompts on three engines over 30 days is 13,500 answers a month, and 350 prompts is 31,500. Profound does not publish prices and is left out of the tables. Treat every figure as directional: enterprise contracts are custom and billed annually, so published self-serve prices show where a negotiation starts, not what you will pay.

Peec AI has the lowest price per prompt in the first table and the lowest monthly price in the second. Scrunch AI's Core plan costs $2.00 per prompt at 125 prompts and five users, and its larger plans are quote-only. Against Rankscale, the only other tool here with a published enterprise price, Peec AI costs 36% less at 150 prompts ($245 against $385) and 37% less at 350 prompts ($495 against $780). Rankscale does include more engines in its price, which Peec AI reserves for Enterprise. On ChatGPT plus both Google surfaces with 15 people logging in, Peec AI is the cheapest of the tools priced in these tables: $495 against $638 for Otterly.AI once Google AI Mode is added, and $780 for Rankscale. Otterly.AI and Rankscale include more engines in their price.

One thing changes these tables: single sign-on. Peec AI, Profound, AthenaHQ, Scrunch AI and Otterly.AI put SSO on Enterprise, and Rankscale puts it on a custom plan. If IT requires SSO, every tool here becomes a quote, and the published prices only show where the negotiation starts. Annual billing takes 15% to 17% off most of these.

Peec AI is a Berlin-based AI search analytics platform with a New York office. It tracks visibility, position, sentiment and share of voice, breaks every answer into the sources the engine read and turns the gaps it finds into prioritised actions. At enterprise scale its pricing is the main difference: users are unlimited on every plan, and Peec does not charge per country or language, with multi-country tracking from the Advanced plan.

Best for: Enterprise teams that want one tool for every market and every team, and need to know which pages to work on, not only where they stand.

Profound suits purchases that have to clear an information security review before anything else. It lists SOC 2, SSO and SAML on Enterprise, and it raised a $96M Series C at a $1B valuation in February 2026, which settles the vendor-risk question quickly.

Best for: Companies where compliance and vendor risk decide the purchase.

AthenaHQ was built by two former Google Search and DeepMind engineers. Its Enterprise plan has the longest feature list of the quote-based tools: SAML and OIDC single sign-on, audit logs, a 2-hour SLA, a dedicated Slack channel and executive dashboards that feed Tableau, Power BI and Looker. An optimisation agent drafts on-page and off-page actions, which suits large companies that have the analysis but not the hands to act on it.

Best for: Enterprises short on people to act on the data, who want BI dashboards and audit logs.

Scrunch AI publishes one self-serve plan and sells everything else through a quote. Core costs $250 a month and includes 125 prompts, 5,000 responses a month, five user licences and Google single sign-on, which is enough for a pilot with a small team.

Best for: Teams that want a published entry price and five users, with nine engines available on Enterprise.

Rankscale is the only tool here where the enterprise price is on the website. Enterprise is $780 a month for 12,000 credits, up to 48,000 answers, with REST API access and a dedicated partner. Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, both Google surfaces, DeepSeek and Mistral are on every paid plan.

Best for: Teams that need a published enterprise price and the widest engine list.

Otterly.AI has the lowest entry price here, with unlimited team members on every plan and unlimited workspaces from the Standard plan, which helps when several business units want their own view. It is a lighter product than the five above, and SSO sits on its Enterprise plan, which starts from 1,000 prompts.

Best for: Business units that want their own workspace at a low price.

The most common mistake is buying for the pilot. A team runs a trial on one brand and one market, picks the tool with the friendliest entry price and finds out in month four that adding other markets, other teams and SSO moves them onto a quote that looks nothing like the trial.

Before you start a trial, write down three numbers: how many people will need to log in within a year, how many markets you sell in, and whether IT will require SSO. Then ask every vendor to price that.

Enterprise AI brand mention tracking is mostly a question of fit with how a large company buys. Peec AI is the strongest overall choice because users and markets do not drive its price, SSO can be enforced, and its source analysis shows what to fix instead of only how you rank.

Profound is the better route when a compliance review decides everything, AthenaHQ when you want BI dashboards and drafted work, Scrunch AI when you want a published entry price with five users, and Rankscale when you need a published enterprise price.

Whichever you pick, price your real workload, ask about SSO first and remember that the tool measures: what moves the number is being on the pages the engines read. The best AI brand mention tracking tools for enterprises are the ones that show you which pages those are.

What does an enterprise AI brand mention tracking tool cost?

Directionally, between $245 and $780 a month on published plans for 150 to 350 daily prompts: Peec AI Pro at $245 and Advanced at $495, Scrunch AI Core at $250 for 125 prompts, Otterly.AI Premium at $489 and Rankscale at $385 to $780. On Peec AI that is $1.41 to $1.63 per prompt with unlimited users. Once SSO is required, every tool here is a custom quote. The spread is driven by users and markets more than by features.

If more than a handful of people will log in, IT will usually ask for it. Every tool here puts SSO on Enterprise or a custom plan, so plan the budget for that contract instead of the self-serve tier.

How many prompts does an enterprise need?

A hundred to a hundred and fifty per brand and market. Start with the questions your sales team hears, then the comparisons buyers make between you and named competitors. More markets multiply the set. More product pages usually should not.

SEO usually owns the measurement. What breaks is the fix, because much of it means getting mentioned on sites you do not control, which sits with PR or communications. Agree that split before you buy.

#10779. Artificial neurons successfully communicate with living brain cells

Engineers at Northwestern University have created printed artificial neurons that go beyond imitation and can directly interact with real brain cells. These flexible, low-cost devices produce electrical signals that closely resemble those generated by living neurons, allowing them to activate biological brain tissue.

In experiments using slices of mouse brain, the artificial neurons successfully triggered responses in real neurons. This result shows a new level of compatibility between electronic devices and living neural systems.

Toward Brain Interfaces and Energy-Efficient AI

This advance moves researchers closer to electronics that can directly interface with the nervous system. Potential uses include brain-machine interfaces and neuroprosthetics, such as implants that could help restore hearing, vision, or movement.

The technology also points toward a new generation of computing systems inspired by the brain. By replicating how neurons communicate, future hardware could perform complex tasks using far less energy. The brain remains the most energy-efficient computing system known, and scientists hope to apply its principles to modern technology.

The study will be published on April 15 in the journal Nature Nanotechnology.

"The world we live in today is dominated by artificial intelligence (AI)," said Northwestern's Mark C. Hersam, who led the study. "The way you make AI smarter is by training it on more and more data. This data-intensive training leads to a massive power-consumption problem. Therefore, we have to come up with more efficient hardware to handle big data and AI. Because the brain is five orders of magnitude more energy efficient than a digital computer, it makes sense to look to the brain for inspiration for next-generation computing."

Hersam is an expert in brain-inspired computing and holds multiple roles at Northwestern University, including the Walter P. Murphy Professor of Materials Science and Engineering at the McCormick School of Engineering. He also is a professor of medicine at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and a professor of chemistry at the Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences. In addition, he serves as chair of the department of materials science and engineering, director of the Materials Research Science and Engineering Center, and a member of the International Institute for Nanotechnology. He co-led the study with Vinod K. Sangwan, a research associate professor at McCormick.

Why the Brain Outperforms Traditional Silicon

Modern computers handle increasing workloads by packing billions of identical transistors onto rigid, two-dimensional silicon chips. Each component behaves the same way, and once manufactured, the system remains fixed.

The brain works very differently. It consists of many types of neurons, each with specialized roles, arranged in soft, three-dimensional networks. These networks are constantly changing, forming and adjusting connections as learning occurs.

"Silicon achieves complexity by having billions of identical devices," Hersam said. "Everything is the same, rigid and fixed once it's fabricated. The brain is the opposite. It's heterogeneous, dynamic and three-dimensional. To move in that direction, we need new materials and new ways to build electronics."

Although artificial neurons have been developed before, most produce overly simple signals. To achieve more complex behavior, engineers typically need large networks of devices, which increases energy use.

Printable Materials Enable Brain-Like Behavior

To better replicate real neural activity, Hersam's team built artificial neurons using soft, printable materials that more closely match the brain's structure. Their approach relies on electronic inks made from nanoscale flakes of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2), which acts as a semiconductor, and graphene, which serves as an electrical conductor. These materials were deposited onto flexible polymer surfaces using aerosol jet printing.

Previously, researchers treated the polymer in these inks as a flaw because it interfered with electrical performance. As a result, they removed it after printing. In this work, the team used that same feature to enhance the device.

"Instead of fully removing the polymer, we partially decompose it," he said. "Then, when we pass current through the device, we drive further decomposition of the polymer. This decomposition occurs in a spatially inhomogeneous manner, leading to formation of a conductive filament, such that all the current is constricted into a narrow region in space."

That narrow conductive path produces a sudden electrical response similar to a neuron firing. The resulting device can generate a wide variety of signals, including single spikes, continuous firing, and bursting patterns, closely resembling real neural communication.

Because each artificial neuron can produce more complex signals, fewer components are needed to perform advanced tasks. This could significantly improve computing efficiency.

Testing Artificial Neurons on Real Brain Tissue

To evaluate whether the artificial neurons could truly interact with living systems, the researchers partnered with Indira M. Raman, the Bill and Gayle Cook Professor of Neurobiology at Weinberg. Her team applied the artificial signals to slices of mouse cerebellum.

The results showed that the electrical spikes matched key biological properties, including their timing and duration. These signals reliably activated real neurons and triggered neural circuits in a way similar to natural brain activity.

"Other labs have tried to make artificial neurons with organic materials, and they spiked too slowly," Hersam said. "Or they used metal oxides, which are too fast. We are within a temporal range that was not previously demonstrated for artificial neurons. You can see the living neurons respond to our artificial neuron. So, we've demonstrated signals that are not only the right timescale but also the right spike shape to interact directly with living neurons."

Low-Cost, Sustainable Manufacturing and AI Implications

Beyond performance, the new approach offers environmental and practical advantages. The manufacturing process is simple and inexpensive, and the additive printing method places material only where it is needed, reducing waste.

Improving energy efficiency is especially important as artificial intelligence systems grow more demanding. Large data centers already consume vast amounts of power and require significant water for cooling.

"To meet the energy demands of AI, tech companies are building gigawatt data centers powered by dedicated nuclear power plants," Hersam said. "It is evident that this massive power consumption will limit further scaling of computing since it's hard to imagine a next-generation data center requiring 100 nuclear power plants. The other issue is that when you're dissipating gigawatts of power, there's a lot of heat. Because data centers are cooled with water, AI is putting severe stress on the water supply. However you look at it, we need to come up with more energy-efficient hardware for AI."

The study, "Multi-order complexity spiking neurons enabled by printed MoS2 memristive nanosheet networks," was supported by the National Science Foundation.

A woman who repeatedly blocks self-driving delivery robots was arrested for refusing to let an Uber Eats machine pass.

Uber Eats introduced autonomous delivery robots in Philadelphia in March 2026, partnering with robotics company Avride to transport food orders through the city’s streets.

On October 14, Marvin encountered an Uber Eats robot near Philadelphia’s Reading Terminal Market, while returning home from a flu shot appointment. She decided to stand in its path until a crowd gathered and police were called to the scene.

#10775. AI swarms could hijack democracy without anyone noticing

A new kind of political threat may be emerging, and it is far less visible than protests or traditional voter manipulation. Researchers warn that highly realistic AI-controlled personas could soon play a major role in shaping public opinion and influencing democratic systems.

A recent policy forum paper published in Science describes how large groups of AI-generated personas can convincingly imitate human behavior online. These systems can enter digital communities, participate in discussions, and influence viewpoints at extraordinary speed. Unlike earlier bot networks, these AI agents can coordinate instantly, respond to feedback, and maintain consistent narratives across thousands of accounts.

Rapid progress in large language models and multi-agent systems has made it possible for a single operator to manage vast networks of AI "voices." These personas can appear authentic, adopt local language and tone, and interact in ways that feel natural to other users.

They are also capable of running millions of small-scale experiments to determine which messages are most persuasive. This allows them to refine their communication strategies in real time and generate what appears to be widespread public agreement. In reality, that consensus is artificially created and designed to influence political discussions.

Deepfakes and fake news signal early risks

Although fully developed AI swarms are still largely theoretical, researchers say there are already warning signs. These include AI-generated deepfakes and fake news outlets that have influenced recent election conversations in countries such as the United States, Taiwan, Indonesia, and India, according to UBC computer scientist Dr. Kevin Leyton-Brown.

At the same time, monitoring organizations have identified pro-Kremlin networks spreading large volumes of online content. This activity is believed to be aimed at shaping the data used to train future AI systems, potentially influencing how those systems behave and what information they prioritize.

Experts warn of growing impact on democracy

Looking ahead, experts believe AI swarms could significantly affect the balance of power in democratic societies. Dr. Leyton-Brown cautioned that these systems are likely to change how people trust information online. "We shouldn't imagine that society will remain unchanged as these systems emerge. A likely result is decreased trust of unknown voices on social media, which could empower celebrities and make it harder for grassroots messages to break through."

Researchers suggest that upcoming elections may serve as a critical test for this technology. The key challenge will be recognizing and responding to these AI-driven influence campaigns before they become too widespread to control.

LinkedIn doesn't publish a price for Recruiter or Recruiter Professional Services. LinkedIn is not standing still: Recruiter now builds search filters from a plain-language description, drafts AI-assisted messages and offers the Hiring Assistant add-on. The limits below are about design, checked against LinkedIn's pages in October 2026.

We checked each vendor's public pricing and product pages in October 2026. Pin is covered first because it spans the widest scope; the others follow in no ranked order.

Pin (pin.com) is an AI recruiting platform that handles candidate sourcing, outreach and interview scheduling in one product. For teams replacing LinkedIn Recruiter, Pin is the most direct one-tool replacement.

The page lists email outreach and no interview scheduling.

hireEZ is a talent acquisition platform that adds sourcing, CRM, outreach, screening and scheduling on top of your ATS. It lists 1B+ profiles across 45+ platforms, email, SMS and InMail engagement, and an AI Scheduler. Team pricing isn't published, and solo recruiters start at $494 a month.

Good for: mid-size and enterprise teams consolidating tools around an existing ATS, though team pricing is unpublished and solo starts at $494 a month.

Gem is a recruiting platform that layers a CRM, AI sourcing, outreach, scheduling and analytics on top of your ATS. #10771. This AI knew the answers but didn’t understand the questions

Psychologists have long debated whether the human mind can be explained by a single, unified theory or if different functions such as attention and memory must be studied separately. Now, artificial intelligence (AI) is entering that debate, offering a new way to explore how the mind works.

In July 2025, a study published in Nature introduced an AI model called "Centaur." Built on standard large language models and refined using data from psychological experiments, Centaur was designed to simulate human cognitive behavior. It reportedly performed well across 160 tasks, including decision-making, executive control, and other mental processes. The results drew widespread attention and were seen as a possible step toward AI systems that could replicate human thinking more broadly.

A more recent study published in National Science Open challenges those claims. Researchers from Zhejiang University argue that Centaur's apparent success may come from overfitting. In other words, instead of understanding the tasks, the model may have learned to recognize patterns in the training data and reproduce expected answers.

To test this idea, the researchers created several new evaluation scenarios. In one example, they replaced the original multiple-choice prompts, which described specific psychological tasks, with the instruction "Please choose option A." If the model truly understood the task, it should have consistently selected option A. Instead, Centaur continued to choose the "correct answers" from the original dataset.

This behavior suggests that the model was not interpreting the meaning of the questions. Rather, it relied on learned statistical patterns to "guess" answers. The researchers compared this to a student who scores well by memorizing test formats without actually understanding the material.

The findings highlight the need for caution when assessing the abilities of large language models. While these systems can be highly effective at fitting data, their "black-box" nature makes it difficult to know how they arrive at their outputs. This can lead to issues such as hallucinations or misinterpretations. Careful and varied testing is essential to determine whether a model truly has the skills it appears to demonstrate.

The Real Challenge: Language Understanding

Although Centaur was presented as a model capable of simulating cognition, its biggest limitation appears to be in language comprehension. Specifically, it struggles to recognize and respond to the intent behind questions. The study suggests that achieving true language understanding may be one of the most important challenges in developing AI systems that can model human cognition more fully.

#10769. Niftski breaks Super Mario Bros. world record in Mario costume as perfect run comes within 2 frames

Super Mario Bros. speedrunner Niftski set a new any% world record on Halloween while dressed as Mario, completing the NES classic in 4:54.299 and moving within two frames of a theoretically perfect run.

The performance lowered Niftski’s previous record of 4:54.332, set in August 2026, by 33 milliseconds. It also pushed the game’s human leaderboard closer than ever to the current benchmark for perfection.

Niftski has spent years pushing Super Mario Bros. toward its limits. In 2021, he became the first player to complete the game in under 4:55, a milestone that was compared to breaking the four-minute mile in speedrunning.

The record chase has since become a battle between Niftski and Brazilian runner LeKukie. LeKukie briefly claimed the world record in June with a 4:54.365 run, cutting the gap to the theoretical limit to six frames before Niftski reclaimed the top spot two months later.

“Only 2 frames (33 milliseconds) stand between this run and absolute perfection / TAS tie,” Niftski wrote after the run.

4:54.299 SMB1 ANY% WORLD RECORD ON HALLOWEEN WHILE LARPING AS MARIO! It doesn't even feel real that I actually achieved this, but here we are. Only 2 frames (33 milliseconds) stand between this run and absolute perfection / TAS tie. 4:54.265 next! pic.twitter.com/S1ZpmEMG4c

That target is based on a tool-assisted speedrun, or TAS, which uses frame-by-frame inputs to determine how quickly the game can theoretically be completed. The relevant benchmark is 4:54.265, created under the same rules used for real-time runs.

There is an even faster TAS time of 4:54.032, but that version uses simultaneous left-and-right inputs that are impossible on a standard NES controller and are banned from human attempts. The 4:54.265 benchmark is therefore treated as the practical theoretical limit for the category.

Super Mario Bros. runs at 60 frames per second, meaning each frame lasts roughly 16.7 milliseconds. The game also uses 21-frame cycles to determine when most levels are completed. That means a runner can lose a few frames in some stages without losing time on the final clock, as long as they still reach the next cycle.

Speedrunner breaks Super Mario Bros world record by the thinnest of margins

Minecraft speedrunner finally sets world record one year after devastating last-second fail

The final level, World 8-4, works differently. It does not offer the same frame-rule cushion, so every successful jump, movement and button press can affect the final result. That is where the remaining gap between Niftski’s record and the TAS benchmark must be erased.

LeKukie remains close behind in the race, and both runners have been streaming attempts at the same impossible-looking goal.

Niftski’s latest record proves that the barrier is no longer theoretical in the way it once seemed. The game has been played for more than 40 years, yet the fastest human performance is now separated from machine-perfect play by less than the blink of an eye.

In 2021, breaking 4:55 felt like the end of what a person could do in Super Mario Bros. Now the question is whether Niftski, LeKukie or another runner can string together the final two frames and complete the first human TAS tie.

#10767. AI lets chemists design molecules by simply describing them

Creating new molecules is one of the toughest tasks in chemistry. Whether the goal is a life-saving drug or a cutting-edge material, each compound must be built through a carefully planned series of reactions. Mapping out these steps requires deep expertise and strategic thinking, which is why chemists often spend years mastering the process.

A major hurdle is retrosynthesis. In this approach, chemists begin with the final molecule they want and work backward to figure out simpler starting materials and possible reaction routes. This involves many decisions, such as selecting the right building blocks, deciding when to form rings, and determining whether sensitive parts of the molecule need protection. While computers can scan enormous "chemical spaces," they still struggle to match the strategic judgment of experienced chemists.

Another challenge involves reaction mechanisms, which describe how reactions proceed step by step through the movement of electrons. Understanding these mechanisms allows scientists to predict new reactions, improve efficiency, and avoid costly trial and error. Although current computational tools can suggest many possible pathways, they often lack the intuition needed to pinpoint the most realistic ones.

Researchers led by Philippe Schwaller at EPFL have developed a new method that uses large language models (LLMs) as reasoning tools for chemistry. Rather than directly generating chemical structures, these models act as evaluators that guide existing computational systems.

The new framework, called Synthegy, combines traditional search algorithms with AI that can interpret chemical strategies written in natural language.

"When making tools for chemists, the user interface matters a lot, and previous tools relied on cumbersome filters and rules," says Andres M Bran, the first author of the Synthegy paper published in Matter. "With Synthegy, we're giving chemists the power to just talk, allowing them to iterate much faster and navigate more complex synthetic ideas."

How Synthegy Improves Retrosynthesis Planning

Synthegy starts with a target molecule and a simple instruction written in everyday language. For example, a chemist might request that a specific ring be formed early or that unnecessary protecting groups be avoided. Standard retrosynthesis software then generates many possible pathways.

Each of these pathways is converted into text and reviewed by a language model. Synthegy scores how well each option matches the chemist's instructions and explains its reasoning. This makes it easier to rank and filter the best routes. By guiding searches with natural language, chemists can quickly focus on strategies that align with their goals.

Understanding Reaction Mechanisms With AI

Synthegy applies a similar method to reaction mechanisms. It breaks reactions down into basic electron movements and explores different possibilities. The language model evaluates each step and steers the search toward pathways that make chemical sense.

The system can also incorporate additional details, such as reaction conditions or expert hypotheses, provided as text. This flexibility allows researchers to refine their analysis and explore more realistic scenarios.

In synthesis planning, Synthgey was able to identify pathways that matched complex strategic instructions. In a double-blind study, 36 chemists provided 368 valid evaluations, and their assessments agreed with the system's results 71.2% of the time on average.

The framework can flag unnecessary protecting steps, judge how feasible reactions are, and prioritize efficient solutions. It also demonstrates that LLMs can operate at multiple levels, from analyzing functional groups to evaluating entire synthetic routes. Larger models performed best, while smaller ones showed more limited abilities.

This research highlights a different way AI can support chemistry. Instead of replacing human decision-making, Synthegy positions language models as guides that help interpret and refine computational results. Chemists can describe their goals in plain language and receive solutions that reflect their strategy.

The approach could speed up drug discovery, improve reaction design, and make advanced tools more accessible to scientists.

"The connection between synthesis planning and mechanisms is very exciting: we usually use mechanisms to discover new reactions that enable us to synthesize new molecules," says Andres M Bran. "Our work is bridging that gap computationally through a unified natural language interface."

#10765. Fanfiction library AO3 could remain offline for up to four weeks after security incident

Archive of Our Own could remain offline for up to four weeks after its nonprofit operator detected a security incident on the fanfiction website.

The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW) said on October 30 that AO3 would remain unavailable while it investigated the incident and determined its scope. The archive first went offline for maintenance on October 29, with the organization initially warning that the work could take at least 12 hours.

AO3 is a nonprofit platform where users publish and read fanfiction, fan art, and other transformative works. OTW said the outage was not caused by data deletion, confirming that works, bookmarks, kudos, and other site content remain safe.

We estimate that service restoration for #AO3 will take around 2 weeks but it could be up to 4 weeks. We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. Refer to our status page for updates: https://t.co/YAyyoTDOpE https://t.co/PUWaHF9M8L

According to OTW’s official update, the organization does not currently believe that AO3’s user database was stolen. However, it said it cannot rule out the possibility while the investigation continues.

The database may contain usernames, email addresses, IP addresses, and hashed versions of users’ passwords. OTW said it does not collect users’ real names, while donor information is stored separately and is not linked to AO3.

The organization advised users to change their passwords on other websites if they reused the same credentials on AO3. It also noted that hashed passwords are stored in a scrambled form, though weak or reused passwords could still be vulnerable to cracking.

OTW’s status page currently estimates that AO3 will be down for a minimum of two weeks and potentially as long as four weeks.

The archive could return sooner in a degraded state, meaning some features may be unavailable or the website may operate in read-only mode. OTW warned that even a limited reopening could be followed by additional unexpected downtime as recovery work continues.

The organization said it will provide further updates through its official channels but may be unable to respond to individual user inquiries while the investigation is ongoing.

#10763. AI Agents Need Idempotency: The Distributed Systems Problem Hiding Inside Agentic AI

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A customer wants a $480 refund for a faulty part of a shipment he received. After waiting for 30 seconds for the payment API to process the refund, the customer support AI sends another request. It ultimately is fulfilled. However, as it turns out, the first request had also been fulfilled. The only thing missing was the notification of the refund for the customer. So the customer received two refunds of $480 each instead of the one he was asking for.

The AI was acting appropriately within its given constraints; the surrounding system couldn’t tell if the initial action had already been taken and failed to deliver the result. A well-known problem in distributed systems is gaining more notoriety as AI-powered agents increasingly perform actions beyond simply generating text. Idempotence is the solution to this problem.

Idempotence means an action can be performed multiple times with the same result as performing it once. This concept is particularly important for an AI agent that issues refunds, creates tickets, sends emails, or updates business applications.

AI agents as distributed software components have simple processes.

Think → choose a tool → call an API → receive a result → decide what to do next.

As we have outlined, many of the agent actions will utilize services and networks that can have issues from time to time. Consider the simple action of asking a payment provider to issue a refund. There are three possible outcomes:

The payment service never gets the request.

The refund went through, and the agent got the answer.

The refund went through, but the agent never received it back.

The most severe case, however, is when the time to complete an operation exceeds the timeout, but the operation does complete successfully. Since there is no answer, the software agent never learns of the operation's successful completion and must attempt to complete the operation again.

Distributed systems have dealt with the issues of unreliable networks for a long time already (retries, duplicate requests, etc.). By introducing agents, we give the software more freedom to choose when and how to proceed.

Consider an agent with these tools: search_customer(), check_inventory(), refund_payment(), send_email(), create_order(), delete_account()

Calling search_customer() twice will usually not cause much trouble.

In other words, an agent runtime should be able to tell if a tool only gets data or makes changes to the outside world. In the second group are things like sending money, getting money back, placing orders, writing messages, making accounts, and changing infrastructure.

There are side effects to these treatments. It's risky to think that agents can just retry every failed tool call as they get access to more business systems.

One common way to handle the duplicate requests issue is to implement idempotency keys.

Idempotency-Key: refund-order-123-run-842

The service stores the idempotency key and the result of processing the associated request.

It allows the refund to be processed the first time the idempotency key is sent to the service by the agent. Thereafter, if the response to the refund is lost and the agent attempts to resubmit the refund with the same idempotency key, the service will recognize that the refund has already been processed and return the previous result to the agent instead of processing another refund.

Many of the world’s leading payment companies, including Stripe, PayPal, and Square, use idempotency keys to allow their customers to safely retry requests.

However, one important rule for agents is that the agent software or workflow system—not the AI model—creates the idempotency key, and it is up to date.

By the time the model retries the same step, the Operation ID will have remained the same. This means the system can recognize the request as another attempt to execute the same action as before and not a new action.

Things could be easy if we could tell the model to ‘remember if it has already issued one of these before issuing another.' But even in the production environment, this approach is not sufficient. The agent could crash. The context could go away. The workflow could be taken off to be executed on another machine. The problem is that the model lacks sufficient information about what has or has not happened in external systems. Instead, the system should keep a record of the execution state outside of the model. The model determines what should happen. The runtime determines safe execution.

Modern agent tools include a name, description, and input parameters for the production system. More importantly, the agent runtime also needs to know about the behavior of the individual tool. For example, ‘refund_order’ modifies the application outside this tool, so the operation must be re-executed with the same actionID used for the initial failure. Also, as an example, refunds larger than $5,000 require manual approval. On the other hand, a ‘search_customer’ action is only a read, so re-execution can occur without human intervention. Based on this information, the OS makes decisions about the danger of the individual tool call. Automatic re-execution is still possible, even if the search fails. However, refunds require a bit more caution to avoid double posting of money. Thus, in addition to the input models for the AI tools used in real life, so-called “execution rules” are also required. These rules state when re-execution, increased security, or human intervention is required.

Suppose an AI agent were to perform the following three actions: 1) Make whole the customer, 2) Send a confirmation email with the order update and a proof, and 3) Check the status of the order in process. We had described how stopping the AI from paying out twice was only half the problem; the system also needed to know where the work had stopped. To that end, we’d like to introduce the concept of durable execution. For durable execution, the agent must do more than simply remember the actions it has taken. We need to keep track of the progress of the actions of the AI. The refund action was marked complete, but the email action was not sent yet. Thus, when the agent is restarted, it continues from where it left off rather than starting over. To create reliable AI agents, we need a few things: stable operation IDs, irrevocable actions, durable state, controlled retries, and logging. There are also cases where one wants to perform a recovery or compensating action (e.g., the agent makes a reservation but then fails to perform the subsequent action). The recovery action would be to cancel the reservation that had been made.

While controls with a person in the loop are mostly suitable for fine-grained actions that cannot be undone, idempotence ensures that an action is not accidentally executed more than once, and human approval is required to decide whether the action should be executed in the first place. This point is illustrated by an example: An employee correctly approves a $10,000 refund. However, the payment request somehow times out and is automatically re-executed several times. Without adequate idempotency security, the customer might end up with even more refunds than intended. Note, however, that a person’s approval cannot prevent double killing in such high-risk agent processes. Therefore, additional decision controls and corresponding execution controls are usually required to ensure that all actions are executed safely and correctly.

There are 5 simple questions that need to be answered before allowing an AI agent to take real-world actions.

Improving the model alone will not make the agent reliable unless we can answer all of these questions.

Much work in AI today focuses on making agents smarter, better at planning, and better to use as tools. But running agents in production has its own problems. API calls time out, processes crash, networks fail, and responses get lost, and the smartest agent can try again and again until it works. These are not new problems. Engineers working on distributed systems have been struggling with these same issues for decades. So long as the AI agent is confined to a simple test environment, of course it can query payment systems, customer information, and corporate tools. But when it is turned loose on the production corporation’s infrastructure (with all the payment systems, customer information, and corporate tools that entails), it must also be reliable. A smart model can figure out that a customer is due a refund. But a strong system can only give that customer a refund once. So the important question to ask of an AI agent before turning loose on it is, "Some powerful new tool: what happens if the action worked?" The answer will tell you whether or not the AI agent is currently able to operate reliably in production.

#10762. Your “um” and pauses could reveal early dementia risk

The way people speak during ordinary conversations could offer valuable insight into brain health, according to new research from Baycrest, the University of Toronto, and York University. Scientists found that subtle speech characteristics, including pauses, filler words such as ('uh,' 'um'), and difficulty retrieving words, are closely connected to executive function, the group of mental abilities involved in memory, planning, attention, and flexible thinking.

The findings provide some of the strongest evidence so far linking natural speech patterns with key cognitive abilities. The work also expands on earlier research showing that older adults who speak more quickly tend to maintain stronger thinking skills over time (Wei et al., 2024).

"The message is clear: speech timing is more than just a matter of style, it's a sensitive indicator of brain health," says Dr. Jed Meltzer, Senior Scientist at Baycrest's Rotman Research Institute and senior author on this study, titled "Natural Speech Analysis Can Reveal Individual Differences in Executive Function Across the Adult Lifespan."

AI Analysis Reveals Hidden Cognitive Clues

For the study, participants were shown detailed images and asked to describe them in their own words. They also completed established tests designed to measure executive function.

Researchers then used artificial intelligence to examine the speech recordings in depth. The AI system detected hundreds of subtle speech features, including the length and frequency of pauses, the use of filler words, and timing-related patterns in speech. These markers consistently predicted how well participants performed on cognitive tests, even after researchers adjusted for factors such as age, sex, and education.

Executive function naturally weakens with age and is often affected during the early stages of dementia. However, standard cognitive testing can be difficult to repeat frequently because it takes time and people often improve simply from becoming familiar with the tests.

Natural speech may offer a simpler alternative. Because speaking is part of daily life, it can be measured repeatedly and unobtrusively on a large scale. Researchers also noted that speech provides valuable insight into processing speed and overall cognitive function in real-world situations, without requiring strict time limits that are common in many traditional cognitive assessments.

The team believes speech analysis could eventually become a practical way to identify people whose cognitive decline is progressing faster than expected and who may face a higher risk of developing dementia.

"This research sets the stage for exciting opportunities to develop tools that could help track cognitive changes in clinics or even at home. Early detection is critical for any cure or intervention, as dementia involves progressive degeneration of the brain that may be slowed," says Dr. Meltzer.

Future Research on Brain Health Monitoring

The researchers say more long-term studies are needed to follow changes in speech over time and distinguish normal aging from the earliest signs of disease. They also suggest that combining speech analysis with other health measures could make early detection of cognitive decline more accurate, practical, and widely available.

This research was supported by the Mitacs Accelerate program and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC).

#10761. YouTuber banned from Massachusetts after allegedly dragging protected great white shark onto beach

A YouTuber has been banned from Massachusetts after allegedly capturing a protected great white shark and dragging it onto a beach for photographs.

Great white sharks are a protected species in Massachusetts, with regulations prohibiting anglers from deliberately attracting or catching them. The restrictions are particularly important around Cape Cod, where large numbers of sharks gather due to the area’s abundant seal population.

Christopher Stefanou, a 30-year-old content creator who operates the YouTube channel LISHARKMAN, is facing multiple criminal charges over an alleged incident involving a great white shark in October 2025.

As per The Independent, Stefanou and his crew spent several days fishing with a European client, allegedly intending to capture a great white shark.

Cape & Islands District Attorney Robert J. Galibois said the group used prohibited equipment, including a drone, to catch a 9.5-foot shark known as Aaron the Shark, which had previously been tagged and monitored by marine researchers.

Prosecutors said the shark was pulled ashore, where members of the group celebrated their catch and took pictures before returning it to the water.

The YouTuber appeared before Barnstable Superior Court on October 21, 2026, to answer charges of animal cruelty to a shark, fishing for shark, mechanical deployment of bait, attempt to capture a shark, and possession of a protected species shark.

Stefanou was released on $10,000 bail but must comply with several restrictions, including handing over his fishing licence and deleting footage connected to the alleged incident.

He has also been forbidden from fishing, using boats, and flying drones in Massachusetts waters. In addition, he cannot return to the state unless attending court.

#10759. New quantum algorithm solves “impossible” materials problem in seconds

Quantum computers and other advanced quantum technologies rely on specialized quantum materials that behave in unusual ways under the right conditions. In some cases, scientists can even create entirely new quantum properties by carefully changing a material's structure. One striking example involves stacking sheets of graphene and twisting them into a moiré pattern, which can suddenly turn the material into a superconductor.

Researchers can arrange these layers into even more complicated structures, including quasicrystals and super-moiré materials. But predicting how these exotic materials will behave is extraordinarily difficult. Quasicrystals are so mathematically complex that simulating them can involve more than a quadrillion numbers, a scale far beyond the reach of today's most powerful supercomputers.

Quantum Algorithm Solves Massive Materials Problem

Scientists at Aalto University's Department of Applied Physics have now developed a quantum-inspired algorithm capable of handling these enormous non-periodic quantum materials almost instantly. Assistant Professor Jose Lado says the work also highlights a promising feedback cycle within quantum technology itself.

"Crucially, these new quantum algorithms can enable the development of new quantum materials to build new paradigms of quantum computers, creating a productive two-way feedback loop between quantum materials and quantum computers," he explains.

The advance could eventually support the development of dissipationless electronics, which conduct electricity without energy loss. Such systems may help reduce the growing heat and energy demands of AI-driven data centers.

The research team was led by Lado and included doctoral researcher Tiago Antão, who served as the paper's main author; QDOC doctoral researcher Yitao Sun; and Academy Research Fellow Adolfo Fumega. Their findings were recently published in Physical Review Letters as an Editor's Suggestion.

The researchers focused on topological quasicrystals, unusual materials that host unconventional quantum excitations. These excitations are especially valuable because they help protect electrical conductivity from disruptive noise and interference. However, they are distributed unevenly throughout the already highly complex structure of a quasicrystal.

Rather than attempting to directly calculate the full structure of the material, the team reformulated the challenge using methods similar to those used by quantum computers.

"Quantum computers work in exponentially large computational spaces, so we used a special family of algorithms to encode those spaces, known as tensor networks, to compute a quasicrystal with over 268 million sites. Our algorithm shows how colossal problems in quantum materials can be directly solved with the exponential speed-up that comes from encoding the problem as a quantum many-body system," Antão says.

At this stage, the work remains theoretical and was carried out through simulations, but researchers say experimental testing and future applications are already coming into view.

"The quantum-inspired algorithm we demonstrated enables us to create super-moiré quasicrystals several orders of magnitude above the capabilities of conventional methods. That is an instrumental step towards designing topological qubits with super-moiré materials for use in quantum computers, for example," Lado says.

Toward Practical Quantum Computing Applications

According to Lado, the algorithm could eventually be adapted to operate on actual quantum computers once the hardware becomes sufficiently advanced.

"Our method can be adapted to run on real quantum computers, once they reach necessary scale and fidelity. In particular, the new AaltoQ20 and the Finnish Quantum Computing Infrastructure can play a significant role for future demonstrations," Lado says.

The findings suggest that studying and designing exotic quantum materials may become one of the earliest practical applications for quantum algorithms and quantum computing systems.

The project also brings together two major areas of Finnish quantum research: quantum materials and quantum algorithms. It is part of Lado's ERC Consolidator grant ULTRATWISTROICS, which focuses on designing topological qubits using van der Waals materials, as well as the Center of Excellence in Quantum Materials QMAT, whose goal is to advance the quantum technologies of the future.

#10757. Influencer who flaunted private jets indicted over alleged $4 million food stamp fraud scheme

A social media influencer has been arrested after allegedly stealing millions of dollars from a government food assistance programme.

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) provides financial support to those with low income, allowing eligible households to purchase groceries using electronic benefit transfer (EBT) cards.

Atlanta-based influencer Mercedes Reshard New, also known as Shawty Dred, has been accused of exploiting the scheme to obtain more than $4 million in benefits between January 2020 and July 2026.

According to the US Department of Justice, the 39-year-old allegedly created more than 350 fraudulent SNAP accounts using stolen identities, before arranging for EBT cards to be delivered to addresses across Atlanta.

Prosecutors also claim that New registered his business, Shawty Dred LLC, as an authorized SNAP retailer, allowing him to withdraw more than $660,000 through transactions involving the fraudulent cards.

After his retailer authorization was revoked in November 2025, New allegedly approached Walmart shoppers and offered to pay for their groceries using EBT cards in exchange for cash.

New was indicted on 63 federal charges, including mail fraud, aggravated identity theft and SNAP fraud, before being arrested on October 13.

During a court appearance on October 22, New pleaded not guilty and was denied bond, with prosecutors arguing that he posed a flight risk. He remains in custody awaiting further proceedings.

#10755. NASA’s new AI space chip could let spacecraft think for themselves

NASA is developing a powerful new computer chip designed to dramatically increase the intelligence and performance of future spacecraft. Through a commercial partnership, the project is creating advanced processing technology capable of helping spacecraft operate more independently during missions far from Earth.

NASA's High Performance Spaceflight Computing project is focused on boosting the computing capabilities of spacecraft used in space exploration. Current missions rely on older processors because they are durable enough to survive the extreme conditions of space. While those chips are dependable, they lack the performance needed for more advanced missions.

The agency says newer and far more capable processors are essential for future autonomous spacecraft, faster onboard scientific analysis, and supporting astronauts during missions to the Moon and Mars.

"Building on the legacy of previous space processors, this new multicore system is fault-tolerant, flexible, and extremely high-performing," said Eugene Schwanbeck, program element manager in NASA's Game Changing Development program at the agency's Langley Research Center, in Hampton, Virginia. "NASA's commitment to advancing spaceflight computing is a triumph of technical achievement and collaboration."

Radiation Hardened Processor Faces Extreme Testing

At the center of the project is a new radiation-hardened processor built to deliver up to 100 times the computing power of today's spaceflight computers while surviving the harsh environment of space. Engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California are running a wide range of tests designed to simulate those conditions.

"We are putting these new chips through the wringer by carrying out radiation, thermal, and shock tests while also evaluating their performance through a rigorous functional test campaign," said Jim Butler, High Performance Space Computing project manager at JPL.

To qualify for spaceflight, the processor must withstand intense electromagnetic radiation and dramatic temperature fluctuations that can damage electronics. High-energy particles from the Sun and deep space can also trigger computer errors that force spacecraft into "safe mode," temporarily shutting down nonessential systems until engineers resolve the issue.

NASA is also testing how the chip handles the challenges of planetary landings.

"To simulate real-world performance, we are using high-fidelity landing scenarios from real NASA missions that would typically require power-intensive hardware to process huge volumes of landing-sensor data," said Butler. "This is an exciting time for us to be working on hardware that will enable NASA's next giant leaps."

Testing at JPL began in February and is expected to continue for several months. Early results have been highly encouraging. According to NASA, the processor is functioning as intended and has shown performance levels roughly 500 times greater than the radiation-hardened chips currently used in spacecraft.

The team also marked the beginning of testing with a symbolic moment by sending an email titled "Hello Universe," referencing the famous introductory messages used during the early days of computer programming.

AI Powered Spacecraft and Deep Space Missions

The processor is being developed jointly by JPL and Microchip Technology Inc., based in Chandler, Arizona. The company is working with NASA through a commercial partnership, and sample chips have already been shared with defense and commercial aerospace partners.

The technology is expected to play a major role in the future of autonomous spacecraft. With onboard artificial intelligence, spacecraft could respond to unexpected situations in real time when communication delays make human control impractical. The chip could also help deep space missions process, store, and transmit massive amounts of scientific data back to Earth more efficiently.

NASA says the processor may eventually support crewed missions to the Moon and Mars as well.

Small Processor With Massive Computing Power

The device is known as a system-on-a-chip (or SoC), meaning it combines the essential components of a computer into a single compact unit. The processor includes central processing units, computational offloads, advanced networking systems, memory, and input/output interfaces.

SoCs are widely used in smartphones and tablets because they are compact and energy efficient. However, NASA's version is designed to survive for years in deep space, potentially traveling millions (or even billions) of miles from Earth without maintenance or repairs.

Once the processor is certified for use in space, NASA plans to integrate it into a wide variety of missions, including Earth orbiters, planetary rovers, deep space probes, and crewed habitats.

The technology could also have benefits on Earth. Microchip plans to adapt the processor for industries such as aviation and automotive manufacturing.

The project is managed by the Space Technology Mission Directorate's Game Changing Development (GCD) program at NASA Langley. The GCD program and JPL, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, oversaw the development process from mission planning and industry studies through final delivery.

NASA JPL selected Microchip as a partner in 2022, and the company funded its own research and development work on the processor.

#10752. Web-Ready AI Images: Formats, Sizes, and srcset Done Right

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI image generation has become a normal part of many web projects. However, the image a model produces is rarely the image a browser should receive. A single large PNG straight from a generator can weigh several megabytes, ignore the visitor's screen size, and slow down your Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) before the page has a chance to impress anyone.

The good news is that the fix is not complicated. If you treat the generated image as a high-quality master file and run it through a small, repeatable pipeline, you can ship images that look sharp on every device and load quickly on slow connections.

This tutorial walks through that pipeline from start to finish: generating at the right size and aspect ratio, choosing modern formats, creating responsive variants with Node.js, writing srcset and sizes correctly, and avoiding the performance mistakes that show up most often in audits.

Image generators are built to produce visually impressive results, not optimized web assets. Their output is usually a single file at one resolution, often in PNG format, and sometimes with an aspect ratio that does not match your layout.

Sending that file directly to the browser creates three problems. First, mobile visitors download far more pixels than their screens can display. Second, PNG is a poor choice for photographic images because its lossless compression produces large files. Third, without width and height information, the browser cannot reserve space for the image, which causes layout shifts as the page loads.

A web pipeline solves all three. You generate one master image, export multiple sizes in modern formats, and let the browser choose the best version for each visitor.

Optimization starts before you export anything. The most efficient pipeline begins with an image that already fits your layout.

Look at where the image will appear and note its aspect ratio at each breakpoint. A full-width hero might use 16:9 on desktop, while a blog thumbnail might use 4:3 or 1:1. Then identify the largest size the image will ever display. For a full-width hero, that could be 1920 pixels wide on large screens, or more if you support high-density displays at wide viewports.

Your master image should be at least as large as that maximum rendered width. Upscaling a small image later almost always introduces blurriness or artifacts.

Modern image-generation models can follow detailed instructions, so describe the technical requirements in your prompt, not just the subject. Specify the aspect ratio, intended display size, visual style, and any areas that need to remain clear for HTML text. The exact controls available will depend on the tool you use, so check its official documentation before building a workflow around a particular feature.

A practical web-focused prompt might read: "hero image of a modern home office at sunrise, soft natural light, calm blue and warm wood tones, clear empty space on the left third for headline text, no text or logos in the image."

That last instruction matters. Avoid baking headlines or buttons into images. Text inside an image cannot be translated, resized for accessibility, or indexed reliably, and it often becomes unreadable at small sizes. Keep text in HTML and use the image for visuals only.

Once you have a master file, decide which formats to serve. For most photographic and illustrative AI images, a combination of AVIF, WebP, and JPEG covers every modern browser while keeping file sizes small.

AVIF typically offers the strongest compression for photographic content and is supported by all major modern browsers, including Safari 16 and later. WebP is slightly less efficient but encodes faster and has near-universal support. JPEG remains a reliable fallback for older browsers and email clients.

Use PNG only when you specifically need lossless quality, such as for sharp-edged graphics or screenshots. Both AVIF and WebP support transparency, so you rarely need PNG for images with transparent backgrounds anymore.

Creating a dozen versions of every image by hand is tedious and error-prone. Instead, script the process. The Sharp documentation explains how to resize images and export them in different formats.

Then create a script that exports several widths in each format:

const widths = [480, 768, 1080, 1440, 1920];

{ ext: 'avif', format: 'avif', options: { quality: 50 } },

{ ext: 'webp', format: 'webp', options: { quality: 75 } },

{ ext: 'jpg', format: 'jpeg', options: { quality: 80, mozjpeg: true } },

for (const { ext, format, options } of formats) {

.resize({ width, withoutEnlargement: true })

Save the file as an ES module, such as build-images.mjs, and run it with Node. The withoutEnlargement option prevents sharp from upscaling the master when a target width is larger than the original.

The quality values above are reasonable starting points, not universal rules. AVIF and WebP quality scales do not map directly to JPEG quality, so compare outputs visually at the sizes your users will actually see. Smooth gradients, which are common in AI-generated skies and backgrounds, are especially prone to banding at aggressive settings.

The MDN responsive images guide explains how srcset and sizes work. The srcset attribute lists available image files and their intrinsic widths. The sizes attribute tells the browser how wide the image will be displayed in the layout. With both pieces of information, the browser can choose the smallest file that still looks sharp on the visitor's screen, including high-density displays.

Here is an example for an image inside an article column that is 720 pixels wide on larger screens and nearly full width on smaller ones:

alt="A modern home office at sunrise with a wooden desk and soft natural light"

The most common mistake is omitting sizes or leaving it at 100vw for images that are not full width. When that happens, the browser assumes the image fills the entire viewport and downloads a much larger file than necessary. Always match sizes to your actual CSS layout.

To offer AVIF and WebP with a JPEG fallback, wrap your image in a picture element. The browser checks each source in order and uses the first format it supports. See the MDN documentation for the picture element for the full syntax.

srcset="dist/hero-768.avif 768w, dist/hero-1440.avif 1440w, dist/hero-1920.avif 1920w"

srcset="dist/hero-768.webp 768w, dist/hero-1440.webp 1440w, dist/hero-1920.webp 1920w"

srcset="dist/hero-768.jpg 768w, dist/hero-1440.jpg 1440w, dist/hero-1920.jpg 1920w"

alt="A modern home office at sunrise with a wooden desk and soft natural light"

The img element is still required. It holds the fallback file, the dimensions, the alt text, and the loading attributes, while the source elements simply provide alternative formats.

If you need a different crop on mobile, such as a square version of a wide hero, add media attributes to your source elements. This technique is called art direction, and it is a good reason to generate or crop a separate master image for small screens rather than relying on CSS to hide important parts of a wide composition.

Always include width and height attributes on your img element. Modern browsers use them to calculate the image's aspect ratio and reserve the correct space before the file downloads, which helps prevent Cumulative Layout Shift. In CSS, set the image to width: 100% and height: auto so it scales responsively while keeping its proportions.

Use loading="lazy" for images below the fold, but never on your hero or other LCP image. Lazy loading your most important image delays it unnecessarily. Instead, add fetchpriority="high" to the LCP image so the browser downloads it early.

Write alt text that describes the image's purpose in context. If an image is purely decorative, use an empty alt attribute so screen readers skip it. Generated images do not come with meaningful descriptions, so this step always requires human judgment.

Use descriptive file names, such as home-office-sunrise-1440.avif, instead of generic names like image-final-v3.png. Clear names make assets easier to manage and give search engines a small amount of extra context.

Be aware of metadata. Some AI image providers, including OpenAI, embed C2PA provenance data that identifies an image as AI-generated. sharp strips most metadata by default, which reduces file size but also removes that provenance information. If transparency matters to your project or your client, recent versions of sharp offer a keepMetadata() method, and you can also disclose AI-generated imagery in captions or credits.

In Chrome DevTools, open the Network panel, filter by images, and resize the viewport or switch to device emulation. Reload the page and confirm that smaller files load on smaller screens. You can also select the image in the Elements panel and check its currentSrc property in the console to see which file the browser actually chose.

Then run Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights. Look for warnings about properly sized images, modern image formats, and LCP.

Not always. AVIF often produces smaller files for photographic content, but it encodes more slowly. Serving both with a JPEG fallback is a safe default.

Four to six widths usually cover most layouts. Choose them based on your breakpoints and the largest rendered size of each image.

Review the current terms of service for the model and the platform you use. Licensing terms can differ between providers and plans.

AI image generation removes much of the cost and time of creating custom visuals, but it does not remove the need for good web engineering. Generate a high-quality master at the right aspect ratio, export responsive variants in modern formats, write accurate srcset and sizes values, protect your LCP and layout stability, and test everything before you ship.

Once the pipeline is scripted, every new image takes seconds to optimize. That combination gives you the creative speed of AI and the performance your visitors expect.
